# AGENTS.md

nstarman/skills is the registry and clearinghouse for the agent skills Nathaniel Starkman
publishes: every skill is registered here, wherever its files live, and listed, validated and
installed from here. Read `.specify/memory/constitution.md` first; it overrides this file.

## Layout

```
<skill>/                         a local skill: SKILL.md, card.json, references/, assets/, scripts/
registry/<name>.json             a skill that lives in another repository (pointer, not a copy)
index.json                       generated: every skill — the contract the website reads
.claude-plugin/marketplace.json  generated: the Claude Code marketplace `nstarman-skills`
README.md                        the skill table and install section are generated (between markers)
scripts/                         skillreg.py (shared), build_index.py, release_zips.py, bump_refs.py
tests/                           python -m unittest discover tests
.specify/, specs/                Spec Kit (v1.1.3); features go specify → plan → tasks → implement
```

A top-level folder with a `SKILL.md` is a local skill; nothing else is (`.claude/`, `.specify/`,
`.github/`, `registry/`, `scripts/`, `specs/`, `tests/` never are).

## Adding a local skill

1. Add `<skill>/SKILL.md` (frontmatter `name` = folder name, `[a-z0-9-]`, ≤ 64 characters;
   `description` ≤ 1024 characters) and `<skill>/card.json`:
   ```json
   { "name": "<skill>", "description": "One or two plain sentences, present tense, for people browsing." }
   ```
2. `python scripts/build_index.py` and commit the regenerated files.
3. Open a pull request (squash merge).

## Registering a skill from another repository

1. Add `registry/<name>.json` — no change is needed in the other repository:
   ```json
   {
     "name": "<name>",
     "description": "One or two plain sentences for people browsing.",
     "source": { "repo": "owner/repo", "path": "skills/<name>", "ref": "main" }
   }
   ```
   `ref` is a branch (the skill tracks it) or a tag (a versioned skill; the weekly bump job keeps it
   current). Register only skills meant for others, not a repository's internal tooling.
2. `python scripts/build_index.py --remote` (checks the skill's `SKILL.md` at `repo`/`path`/`ref`),
   commit, open a pull request.

## Generated files and checks

Never edit `index.json`, `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` or the README's generated sections by
hand: change the skill or the registry entry and run `python scripts/build_index.py`.
`check.yml` runs on every pull request and push: unit tests, `build_index.py --check --remote`
(formats, unique names, every `SKILL.md` at its real location, claude.ai limits, freshness) and
`claude plugin validate .`.

## End-to-end tests of a skill

A skill that documents a fast-moving tool can have a behaviour test under
`tests/skills/<skill>/` (a `run.sh` plus fixtures) and its own workflow
(`.github/workflows/test-<skill>.yml`) that runs it weekly against the latest upstream release and
on pull requests touching the skill. These tests may install third-party tools (Quarto, Playwright,
Chrome, Sphinx, Zensical); the standard-library rule is for `scripts/`. A scheduled failure opens an
issue, and the skill's `UPDATING.md` says how to bring it current. Today: `quarto-revealjs`,
`diataxis`. Every script a skill ships also has a unit test in `tests/test_*.py` (stubs on `PATH`
stand in for ssh, Slurm and the like), so `check.yml` covers it.

Everything here is public, not only the skills: no personal details (usernames, home paths, password-manager items, project or
paper names, record IDs); use placeholders such as `<kerb>` or `op://<vault>/<item>`. Before a
pull request, run `python scripts/personal_check.py`. It reads its patterns from
`~/.config/skills/personal-strings.txt`, kept outside the repository because the list is itself
personal, so CI skips it.

## Releases and zips

Versions are dates, as in figpress-apps and syw-site: a release is `vYYYY.MM.DD`; a second release on the
same day is `vYYYY.MM.DD.2`, and so on. Every release is a complete snapshot of all skills, so
nothing is backported here.

`release.yml` builds one zip per skill (the skill's folder, without `card.json`; external skills at
their ref) on every push to `main`, weekly and by hand, and publishes a release tagged
`vYYYY.MM.DD` only when a zip changed. `https://github.com/nstarman/skills/releases/latest/download/<name>.zip`
is the stable link (it 404s until the first release exists).

`bump-refs.yml` runs weekly: for tag-pinned entries it opens (or updates) one pull request moving
them to their repository's latest release (date tags sort after older semver tags, e.g. figpress-apps'
`v2026.10.30` after `v0.2.0`). Pull requests opened by `GITHUB_TOKEN` do not trigger
CI; the job validates and puts the output in the pull request — re-run checks before merging.

## How it reaches the website

[nstarman/nstarman.github.io](https://github.com/nstarman/nstarman.github.io) reads
`index.json`; nothing here pushes to it. Its weekly `refresh-skills.yml` (or a manual run) runs
`scripts/collect-skills.mjs`, which writes `config/skills.json` for the Agent Skills section of
`/tools/` and opens a pull request on the site when it changed.

`index.json` (schema 1) is a contract: adding an optional field keeps `schema: 1`; removing or
renaming a field, or changing its meaning, makes it `schema: 2` and must be coordinated with the
collector, which refuses an unknown schema rather than showing a broken section.

# Diátaxis documentation refactoring

Paths below are relative to this skill's own directory, not the user's project.

## Which job is this?

| Request | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| A whole docs tree; "our docs are a mess" | Full workflow: audit → map → refactor |
| "Split this page" / "where does this belong?" | Skip the scanner. Compass the page section by section, then apply moves |
| "Write a tutorial / how-to / reference page for X" | Skip phases 1–2. Read `references/modes.md` for that mode and write. Tutorials: run the preflight below first |
| Docs from scratch | Greenfield — no audit, no map. Tree + landing pages are the deliverable |

## The compass

Two questions, asked of a sentence, a section, a page, or a site:

1. Am I serving **action** or **cognition**?
2. Does this user need **acquisition** (study) or **application** (work)?

| If the content…  | …and serves the user's… | …then it must belong to… |
| ---------------- | ----------------------- | ------------------------ |
| informs action   | acquisition of skill    | a tutorial               |
| informs action   | application of skill    | a how-to guide           |
| informs cognition| application of skill    | reference                |
| informs cognition| acquisition of skill    | explanation              |

**Apply it at section scale, not page scale.** Real documentation rarely contains a misfiled
page; it contains a how-to guide with three paragraphs of explanation wedged into step 4 and a
table of every config flag at the bottom. A page-level audit records "how-to, fine." A
section-level audit records "how-to + explanation §2 + reference §5 — three destinations." The
second one is a work order; the first is a shrug.

## Ground rules

These bind on every job, and two of them are what separates a real refactor from a
plausible-looking one.

**Facts move; they are not manufactured.** A restructure relocates existing content. It does not
license inventing API surface, config keys, error strings, defaults, version matrices or CLI
flags to make a table look finished. When the source does not supply a fact the destination
seems to need, write `TODO(verify): <what is missing>` and list it in the summary. A reference
table with four real rows is worth more than one with twelve rows of which eight are guesses,
because the guesses are indistinguishable from the truth to every future reader. This pressure
is strongest in reference, where completeness feels obligatory — resist it there hardest.

**Move the machinery with the content.** A code block is not just its text. When you EXTRACT or
SPLIT, carry everything the block depended on: its imports, its `try`/`except` wrapper, doctest
skip markers and directives, fixtures, and any earlier block that defined a name it uses. A
snippet that ran inside its old page and raises `NameError` inside its new one is the most common
way a "verbatim" restructure breaks a project's test suite — and the page still looks right.

**A page moved unchanged can still be wrong.** Verbatim relocation preserves the source's
mistakes. When you move a page that gives commands — a contributing guide, an install page, a
testing page — check its commands against what the repo actually uses now (`nox` vs `tox`, PEP
735 dependency groups vs extras, task names, paths). Fix them or mark them `TODO(verify)`; do not
carry a broken command into a nicer folder and record the move as "mechanical, no contaminants".

**Never claim a verification you did not perform, and keep the claims out of the docs.** If you
write "expected output" in a tutorial, either run the command and paste the real bytes, or mark
the block as illustrative and say in the summary that it needs replacing. Never assert
determinism ("your numbers will match these") for output you have not observed.

Verification claims belong in your summary, naming the exact command you ran — never baked into
a file that ships: not a comment in `conf.py` or `zensical.toml`, not a line of page prose. A
config comment saying "verified against version X" is false the moment anything changes, and
nobody will ever go back and delete it. The summary is dated and disposable; the repo is not.

**Every file you create either has real content or is declared missing.** No silent stubs. A page
you did not write must appear on its section landing page under "Not yet written" *and* in the
summary's gap list with a line on what it needs. A tree of confident-looking empty files with a
summary that does not mention them is the worst output this skill can produce — a reader clicks
Explanation, finds one stub, and stops trusting the nav. Forced symmetry is where stubs come
from: one page per mode per feature yields four thin pages where one good one belongs. Modes
need not be balanced; a healthy doc set often has fifteen how-tos and two tutorials.

**One canonical home per fact.** Concepts get one explanation page; *atomic facts* get one table
row. A value with a type and a default — `runtime.workers`, "clamped above 64", the list of
supported formats — belongs in exactly one reference table, and everywhere else links to it.
Duplicated facts drift, and reference↔reference duplication is the worst kind because both
copies look authoritative. Note that the same fact often hides under two names: `--log-level` in
a CLI reference and `log.level` in a config reference are one fact, not two. The scanner's
**Facts asserted on more than one page** section finds these — run it over the *finished* tree,
not just the source, because a restructure is where duplicates get created. It matches table rows
and definition lines only, so a clean report means "no duplicated table row", not "no duplicated
fact"; prose duplication still needs your eyes, and claiming otherwise on the strength of a silent
tool is its own kind of false verification.

## Tutorial preflight

Run this **before writing a line** of any tutorial. A tutorial that cannot be completed is not a
flawed tutorial, it is a failed one — you are required to be present but condemned to be absent,
so nobody is there to rescue the learner.

- [ ] Runs on a laptop with nothing but the product installed. **No cloud account, no API key, no
      bucket, no hosted database, no signup, no paid resource.**
- [ ] Needs no network beyond installing the product. If the product's whole point is a remote
      service, use its local/offline/sandbox mode or a fixture — and if none exists, narrow the
      tutorial to the part that runs locally and name the gap.
- [ ] Zero placeholders. `YOUR_API_KEY`, `<your-project>`, "your region" each make it fail.
- [ ] Zero branches. No per-platform sections, no "if you prefer", no optional steps.
- [ ] Every step prints something, and you have written what it prints — from an actual run
      where you could run it.
- [ ] Anything you assert about state (a cache hit, a timing improvement) is consistent with what
      the learner actually did in the preceding steps.
- [ ] The learner ends holding something they made and can re-run from clean.

**Installation is not a lesson.** Test on the artifact, not the intent: at the end of the page,
has the learner *built or run something*, or is the software merely installed? If the latter, it
is `how-to/install.md` whatever the title says. A tutorial installs in step one and spends the
rest of the page making something work; a page whose final step is "verify the installation
succeeded" has no lesson in it.

**Before writing or rewriting any page, read `references/modes.md`** for that mode. It carries
the constraints, language patterns and failure modes that decide whether the page works.

## Workflow

**Map everything; execute in slices.** Reading and classifying the whole tree is cheap and
read-only, and without it your local decisions fight each other. Editing is expensive and hard to
reverse, so ship it in increments that each stand alone. (Diátaxis's "don't try to work on the
big picture" argues against withholding fixes pending a grand plan — not against knowing what
you have.)

### Phase 1 — Inventory and audit

Run the bundled scanner first; it gives you a work-ordered starting point and the seam list:

```bash
python <skill-dir>/scripts/docs_inventory.py <docs-root> --format md --out audit/inventory.md
```

Its **Seams** table — sections whose signals disagree with their page — is the output that
matters; those are the EXTRACT and SPLIT targets. Treat its `reads as` column as a prompt for the
compass, never a verdict: it counts words and cannot know what a user needs.

Then read the pages, working down each heading tree with the compass. Alongside, settle four
site-level questions:

- Where does a brand-new user actually land, and does anything there teach them?
- **Is there any real tutorial?** Usually there is not — there is a "Getting Started" page that
  is an installation how-to. This is the most common gap in a doc set, and it is a writing job,
  not a moving job.
- Where does reference live, and is it generated, hand-written, or both?
- What is **not practitioner documentation at all**? Changelog, release notes, contributor guide,
  ADRs, governance, support, licence. Legitimate, and outside the four modes — give them their
  own top-level home (`about/`) rather than mangling them into a quadrant.

### Phase 2 — The migration map

One table covering every page; template in `assets/audit-template.md`.

**Every source file gets exactly one row and one destination. No blanks.** The legal destinations
are: one of the four mode sections; the non-practitioner section; *dissolved into* N named pages;
or *deleted, with a redirect*. There is no fifth option and no "leave it at the root." A page
that will not fit is either two things fused (SPLIT) or not practitioner documentation. Before
calling the map done, count its rows against the source file count and state both numbers.

Order the work by leverage: entry points first (a contaminated entry point costs more than a
contaminated appendix), then the most mixed pages, then missing tutorials, then the rest.

**Greenfield is the exception to all of this.** Starting from nothing there is no audit and no
map; the tree plus the landing pages *are* the deliverable, so you do create the four sections
before the content exists. Write the landing pages fully, in reader terms — they are not stubs.
Everything unwritten goes in a "Not yet written" list on its section landing page and in the
summary. Do not generate placeholder pages for content you are not writing.

Present the map, then proceed — do not stop and wait unless the user asked for a plan only. Stop
for confirmation on exactly one class of action: deletions and anything else that loses the only
copy of content. Moves and rewrites are recoverable from git; deletions are not.

### Phase 3 — Refactor

One destination page at a time, finished before the next: apply the moves, rewrite in the target
mode's voice, fix the links.

## The refactoring moves

| Move | What it does | Typical trigger |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **SPLIT** | One page becomes two or more, one per mode | Page scores high on two modes |
| **EXTRACT** | Lift a passage out and rehome it, leaving a link — with its imports, skip markers and setup | Explanation embedded in a how-to |
| **DRAIN** | Pull scattered facts out of prose into a reference table | Options/defaults mentioned inline across a narrative |
| **MOVE** | Whole page is fine, wrong section | Correctly written, misfiled |
| **RETITLE** | Fix the title so the mode is legible from the nav | "Application performance monitoring" → "How to integrate application performance monitoring" |
| **DEMOTE** | Tutorial → how-to guide | It assumes competence and solves a task; it never taught anything |
| **PROMOTE** | How-to → tutorial | It is a newcomer's first contact and needs to build confidence |
| **LINK** | Replace duplicated content with a cross-reference | The same explanation or default appears in three places |
| **MERGE** | Several fragments become one coherent page | Three thin how-tos that are really one task |
| **STUB** | Create a section landing page | A new section needs an entry point |
| **DELETE** | Remove it, redirect the URL | Superseded or duplicated verbatim. Needs sign-off |

EXTRACT and DRAIN do most of the real work. A doc set "reorganized" without them has only moved
contaminated pages into tidier folders.

## Contamination smells

| Smell | What it means | Move |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Page called "Getting Started" that only installs things | An installation how-to, not a tutorial | DEMOTE, and note the missing tutorial |
| "You can either A or B, depending on…" inside a tutorial | Choice — kills tutorial flow | Pick one; EXTRACT alternatives to a how-to |
| A tutorial with troubleshooting sections | It does not reliably work; tutorials must not fail | Fix the tutorial; move edge cases to a how-to |
| "Note: this only works if…" scattered through prose | Reference facts homeless in narrative | DRAIN |
| A table of every option mid-walkthrough | Reference fused to a tutorial or how-to | DRAIN + LINK |
| An "Advanced" or "Guides" section | Unsorted overflow bucket, not a mode | Re-audit its contents individually |

## Examples, architecture, toolchain

- **Writing or reviewing examples and code blocks** → `references/examples.md`. An example that
  would be excellent in one mode is a defect in another; that file has the per-mode rules and the
  practices that stop examples rotting.
- **Planning the tree, writing landing pages, nav depth, cross-linking, a second dimension
  (products/roles/platforms), or keeping the structure from decaying** → `references/architecture.md`.
  Templates: `assets/landing-page-template.md`, `assets/contributing-diataxis.md`.
- **Sphinx / MyST** → `references/sphinx-myst.md`. **Zensical** → `references/zensical.md`.
  Other stacks: the modes and moves are unchanged; find their equivalents for nav, section index
  pages, cross-file links, and redirects.

## Don't break links

A restructure changes every URL, and inbound links live in issue trackers, Stack Overflow and
bookmarks you cannot edit. Three rules:

1. **Confirm the stack can redirect before anything moves.** If it cannot (older Zensical
   releases cannot), say so and agree a mitigation — host-level rules, generated stub pages, or
   keeping URLs stable — rather than silently shipping breakage.
2. **Every old URL gets a redirect, fragments included**, since deep links carry anchors. Generate
   them from the map with `scripts/make_redirect_stubs.py` rather than by hand.
3. **Make broken links fail the build**, and verify before you claim it. `scripts/check_links.py`
   checks the source tree stack-agnostically; the toolchain files cover CI wiring. Pick one
   redirect mechanism and make it work — three overlapping half-configured layers is worse than
   one that is tested.

## The repo references the docs too

This is the failure that survives every docs-only check, and it is the one most likely to
embarrass whoever ships your work. A restructure can pass the link checker, build clean, and
still break the project, because things outside `docs/` name doc paths:

- **tests** that read a doc file (a spec/code drift gate parsing `docs/spec.md` — delete that
  file and the whole suite aborts at collection, so every test is now red)
- **`noxfile.py` / `tox.ini` / `Makefile`** targets, and generators like `sphinx-apidoc -o docs/api`
  which will happily recreate the directory you just dissolved
- **CI workflows** naming doc paths
- **`README.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`** — every stale link here is a 404 on GitHub, and
  `AGENTS.md` is usually the first file a new contributor or agent is pointed at
- **`.readthedocs.yaml`**, packaging metadata, and docs inside sub-packages

Run the bundled checker over the whole repo, not just the docs tree:

```bash
python <skill-dir>/scripts/check_repo_refs.py <repo-root> \
    --old-docs <pristine-copy-of-docs> --new-docs docs/
```

Then **run the project's own gate** — its test suite, its doctest/Sybil run over the docs, its
docs build. Not a substitute harness you wrote: the real one, the way CI runs it. If it will not
run, work at it before you conclude it cannot — a missing interpreter version, an editable
install, or a dependency group is usually the whole obstacle, and "I could not run the tests" is
a claim you have to earn just like any other. When it genuinely cannot run, say exactly what
stopped you.

Compare the example count before and after. A restructure that quietly drops fifty executed
examples has removed test coverage, whatever the page count says.

## Deliverables

1. `audit/inventory.md` — scanner output.
2. `audit/migration-map.md` — the per-page table, including redirects (`assets/audit-template.md`).
3. The refactored pages, landing pages, and updated nav config.
4. A summary following `assets/summary-template.md` — which requires a *Facts I invented or
   inferred* section and a *Gaps found and not filled* section. Both are mandatory; write "none"
   only if it is true.

## Before you say you're done

- Map rows = source file count, and both numbers are stated.
- No practitioner page sits outside the four mode sections.
- Every created file has real content or appears in the gap list.
- Every moved URL has a redirect, or the no-redirect mitigation is written down.
- `check_links.py` passes, and the scanner reports no duplicated table rows across the new tree
  (prose duplication you checked by reading).
- `check_repo_refs.py` is clean: nothing outside `docs/` still points at a page you moved.
- The project's own test/doctest/build gate runs green, or you have said precisely what stopped
  you from running it. Example counts did not silently drop.
- Every redirect target actually resolves in the new tree. A stub that 404s is worse than no
  stub, and an anchor map that rewrites paths it should have left alone manufactures 404s on
  links that used to work.
- Any build or run you claim to have done, you actually did — and the claim is in the summary,
  not in a shipped config comment or page.
- Every tutorial passes the preflight.
- No fifth mode in the nav.

--- name: engaging-hybrid-compute description: Split a research project between a local machine and MIT's Engaging (ORCD) cluster, with code and results kept in sync through a private git repo. Light work (editing, plotting, quick checks) stays local; heavy compute runs as Slurm jobs. Use when the user mentions Engaging, ORCD, orcd-login, sbatch/squeue on the MIT cluster, queue priority or fair share, moving runs to the cluster, syncing results back, or a project that already has this setup (a cluster clone, a deploy key, slurm/ scripts). --- # Local ↔ Engaging hybrid compute, synced through a private git repo One repo, two working copies: ``` local machine GitHub (private repo) Engaging (cluster clone) edit, commit, push ───────────────▶ origin ◀───── pull --rebase (deploy key) ───── login node: git pull, uv sync, sbatch pull --rebase, plot ◀─────────────── ◀──── push_results.sh (figures, small arrays) ── after jobs finish ``` - **Code** is written locally, committed and pushed. The cluster only pulls. - **Results** that are cheap to regenerate and small (figures, small `.npz`/`.json`, result tables) are committed *on the cluster* by `push_results.sh` and pulled locally. - **Big things** (raw simulation snapshots, caches, `.venv`, Slurm logs) never go in git. Move them with `rsync` only when needed. - **Heavy compute only on the cluster.** Locally: editing, plotting, reading results, checks that take seconds. **Assumes 1Password** on the local machine: its SSH agent holds the cluster key and signs commits, so a locked 1Password shows up as SSH or commit failures. Other agents work, but `setup.md` is written for 1Password. Read `setup.md` (next to this file) for the one-time setup. The rest of this file is the daily workflow and the rules. ## Connecting (SSH key + Duo + ControlMaster) An SSH key replaces the password but **does not skip Duo**. The way around it is a ControlMaster socket: the user opens one connection (one Duo push), and every later `ssh`, `scp` or `rsync` reuses it for the `ControlPersist` window (e.g. 8 h). 1. Check: `ssh -O check `, where `` is the `~/.ssh/config` host, e.g. `orcd-login`. 2. If "Master running": run everything as `ssh -o BatchMode=yes ''`. `BatchMode` makes it fail fast instead of hanging on a Duo prompt. 3. If not, the user has to reconnect. Either they run `ssh ` in their own terminal and approve Duo, or they have the gated helper from `setup.md`. Call it only as `engaging-connect`, never by path or through a wrapper, so its permission rule fires. - Before running the helper, tell the user a permission prompt and a Duo push are coming, with a push notification if your harness has one, so they can approve from their phone when away from the machine. - **At most one reconnect attempt per need. Never loop.** Repeated failed attempts can trigger a Duo lockout. - If key auth is refused instantly with a message about logging in to the web portal, the user must first log in to OnDemand (https://orcd-ood.mit.edu) in a browser. Key auth appears to need a recent OnDemand login (about a day). Ask them; don't retry. The open socket is a full shell on the user's account. Treat every command as if the user typed it, and keep to the rules below even when nothing prompts. Never: - run `ssh -O exit `, which kills the user's shared socket; - run plain `ssh ` without `BatchMode=yes`, which hangs on the Duo menu; - touch `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` on the cluster. ## Rules - **No compute on the login node.** Allowed there: `git`, `uv sync` (installs), `rsync`, `sbatch`/`squeue`/`sacct`/`scancel`, reading logs, tiny file inspection. Everything else goes in a Slurm job (`mit_quicktest` for anything short). - **Free tier only** unless the user explicitly asks otherwise: partitions `mit_quicktest`, `mit_normal`, `mit_normal_gpu`, `mit_preemptable`; no paid QOS, reservations or rentals. Before every `sbatch`, check the job against the free caps (wall time, CPUs, GPUs, memory per user, as the ORCD docs list them). If it only fits a paid tier, don't submit: say which limit it exceeds and what the paid option would cost (current prices in the ORCD docs), and offer free alternatives (split it, checkpoint and resubmit, a job array, or `mit_preemptable` with `--requeue`). - **Ask the user before:** - jobs beyond the project's agreed size, for example > 12 h, more than ~20 array tasks or > 32 CPUs per task (agree the thresholds per project); - GPU jobs, unless agreed; - deleting anything on the cluster; - changing pinned dependencies. - **Keep the repo private.** Never commit secrets, keys or tokens. `push_results.sh` commits every `.json` in an experiment folder, so no credentials go in those folders, and job logs print only named switches, never the whole environment. - **Commit signing:** if a commit fails because the signing agent is locked (1Password's SSH agent), ask the user to unlock 1Password. Never bypass signing (`--no-gpg-sign`, changing config). - **If something breaks, stop and report.** Don't quietly fall back to running locally or to a different dependency source. ## The daily loop 1. **Local:** edit → commit → push. 2. **Cluster:** update the clone, then **verify the code arrived** before submitting: ```bash ssh -o BatchMode=yes 'cd && git pull -q --rebase --autostash && git log --oneline -1 && grep -c "" ' ``` Run `uv sync --frozen` only if the lockfile changed (it's an install, so fine on the login node). *Why verify:* if the local commit silently failed (e.g. signing), the cluster runs the old code and you only find out hours later. 3. **Submit** with `sbatch`, usually the generic array script `scripts/run_modes.sh` (one mode per task). Give jobs **descriptive names**: they're how you watch them. 4. **Watch** by job name, not by a list of IDs (see Monitoring). 5. **Collect:** on the login node, `scripts/push_results.sh ""` commits figures and small arrays from the experiment folders and pushes. 6. **Local:** check what the cluster pushed, then pull: ```bash git fetch -q && git log --stat HEAD..@{u} ``` Cluster commits should touch only result files in experiment folders. If one changes code, scripts or config, stop and tell the user before pulling: the deploy key may be misused. Then `git pull --rebase`, plot, analyse and write notes. ## Submitting jobs well - **Settings via environment, passed with `--export=ALL,KEY=val,...`.** `--export` **splits on commas**, so never put a comma inside a value: `KAPPAS=8,4,2,1` arrives as `KAPPAS=8`. Use another separator (`8:4:2:1`). - **Every switch that changes results must appear in the output filename.** Two jobs that differ only in an env var otherwise overwrite each other's output. Add the tag to the code that writes outputs *before* submitting. - **Print the full configuration on the first lines of each job log.** Then a typo in a mode string shows up when you first look at the log. Check the first log lines of one task before trusting a whole batch. - **Smoke test on `mit_quicktest`** (15 min) after any environment change: imports, one small run, compare with a local result. - **Size memory from history:** `sacct -j -o JobID,Elapsed,MaxRSS,ReqMem`. Per-user caps (e.g. 96 CPUs and 386 GB on `mit_normal`) mean big-memory jobs run a few at a time; request what you need, not the maximum. - **Chain dependent steps:** `sbatch --dependency=afterok: ...`. Check that the upstream result is actually usable before relying on the chain; e.g. a fit that converged to the wrong solution still exits 0. - **Jobs read the code when they *start*, not when you submit.** Pulling new code on the cluster changes what *queued* jobs will run. Pull only when the change is backward compatible for queued jobs (new option with an unchanged default), or wait until they've started. - **Logs:** `#SBATCH -o slurm/logs/%x-%j.out` (arrays: `%x-%A_%a.out`). The directory must exist before `sbatch`. - **Thread counts:** inside a job, `os.cpu_count()` reports the whole node, not your allocation. Pin threads (`OMP_NUM_THREADS`, `XLA_FLAGS`, etc.) to `$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK` if oversubscription shows up. - **Tools installed in `~/.local/bin` (e.g. `uv`) aren't on the non-interactive `PATH`.** Call them by full path in job scripts. ## Fair share: fewer, more targeted jobs Queue priority on Engaging is mostly **fair share**: how much of your share of the cluster you have used lately. Every CPU-hour you run lowers the priority of your next job. A day of broad sweeps can leave the user near the bottom of the queue for a week or more. So treat CPU-hours as a budget, not as free. **How it works** (check the live values; sites retune them): - `scontrol show config | grep ^Priority` gives the weights. Within one partition the partition term is the same for everyone, so fair share is the main factor that differs between users. Job size and age add only a little. - Usage decays with `PriorityDecayHalfLife` (7 days at the time of writing), so last week's runs still count. - Billing is per allocated CPU × elapsed time (`scontrol show partition

| grep TRES`). Requested CPUs are charged **even when idle**. Memory is not billed, but it still limits how many of your jobs run at once. - `sshare -l -u $USER` shows `LevelFS = share / usage`; below 1 means over your share. `FairShare` is your **rank** among all users from 0 to 1, not a ratio: 0.03 means about the bottom 3%. - `sprio -j ` breaks one pending job's priority into these factors. **Before submitting, ask what question the batch answers**, and run the smallest set of jobs that answers it: - **Screen, then expand.** Run one seed and one configuration first, or a short pilot on `mit_quicktest`. Add seeds or arms only for the variants that look informative. Don't launch the full grid "to have it". - **Don't run what's already decided.** Drop arms that earlier results have already ruled out, and skip any job whose output file already exists. - **Gate dependency chains on usefulness, not only exit code.** `afterok` fires on a fit that converged to the wrong solution. Have the upstream step exit non-zero if its result is unusable, so the downstream jobs never start. - **Cancel jobs as soon as they stop being informative.** Ask first if the user started them. - **Pack small runs that share setup into one job.** For example, loop over modes in one process. Imports, environment start-up and JIT compilation (JAX etc.) are then paid once instead of per task. This saves real CPU-hours, unlike splitting the same work differently. **Right-size every request:** - `-c`: only what the code actually uses. Check `sacct -j -o Elapsed,TotalCPU,AllocCPUS`: if TotalCPU ≪ Elapsed × AllocCPUS, most of the allocated CPUs sat idle and were still billed. - `-t`: a realistic limit from past runs plus a margin, not the partition maximum. Charging uses elapsed time, so this doesn't change cost. It does change wait: the backfill scheduler slots jobs with **short, accurate limits** into idle gaps ahead of higher-priority jobs. That is how jobs with low priority still start while CPUs sit idle. - `--mem`: from `MaxRSS` history. It isn't billed, but too much memory stops jobs from packing onto nodes. **When priority is already low:** - Submit the most informative job first. Hold the rest (`scontrol hold ` / `scontrol release `) instead of queueing everything at once, so the job that matters runs first. Holding doesn't restore priority; only not running does. - Prefer `mit_quicktest` (15 min) for anything that fits. Tiny jobs on any partition backfill easily. - Tell the user roughly how long recovery takes: LevelFS reaches 1 after usage decays by a factor of 1/LevelFS, which takes about `half-life × log2(1/LevelFS)` with no new runs. ## Monitoring Use `scripts/watch_jobs.sh ` (or the same loop inline) as a background task: - **Match jobs by name with `squeue --me -h -o %j | grep -cE ''`.** Don't use `squeue -j id1,id2,...`: one invalid or finished ID makes `squeue` print nothing, which looks like "all done". - **Treat an ssh failure as a failure, not as "0 jobs left".** A dropped socket otherwise ends the watch early. - Sleep 5–20 minutes between checks. When the jobs disappear, print the result lines from the logs. Useful checks: ```bash squeue --me -o "%i %j %T %M %l %r" # state, elapsed, limit, pending reason sacct -X -n -S -o JobID%14,JobName%22,State%12,Elapsed scontrol show res | grep -E "ReservationName|StartTime" # maintenance windows ``` ## Maintenance windows and pending reasons - `ReqNodeNotAvail, Reserved for maintenance`: a reservation (e.g. monthly maintenance) is coming and your job's time limit would overlap it. If the job really needs less time, lower its limit so it fits before the window: `scontrol update JobId=_0 TimeLimit=03:00:00` (users can lower, not raise, limits). - `QOSMaxCpuPerUserLimit`: you're at your per-user cap; jobs start in waves. To free slots, cancel your own jobs that have become uninformative. Ask before cancelling anything the user started. - `Priority`: normal queueing. A long wait under `Priority` usually means low fair share (see Fair share). - `Dependency`: waiting on an upstream job. ## Bookkeeping - Keep a running notes file in the repo (decisions, findings, job IDs, what each result means) and commit it often in small logical commits. - Keep a cluster notes file for setup facts and gotchas, and append new ones. - Each experiment gets its own folder (`NN_short_name/`) with a runnable script, so `push_results.sh` can glob results by folder. - At the end of the project phase, revoke the deploy key in the repo settings.

name: quarto-revealjs
description: Use whenever someone asks to make a talk, presentation, slide deck or slides (even without naming Quarto), and when making, editing or checking a Quarto reveal.js presentation (`format: revealjs`, `.qmd` slides) that must work offline or be archived as one self-contained HTML file plus a PDF; when a deck shows raw TeX, loads MathJax, KaTeX or plotly.js from a CDN, or breaks without internet; when adding speaker notes, fragments (including inside equations), auto-animate, backgrounds, video, Plotly figures from Python cells, or an interactive single-file HTML app (iframe) to slides; when printing a deck to PDF; or when asked which reveal.js features Quarto supports and how to write them.
---

# Offline, archivable reveal.js decks with Quarto

The goal: a deck that opens in any browser for decades with no network. One `.qmd` source renders to
one self-contained HTML file (`embed-resources: true`), and a PDF printed from that same HTML is the
backup. A default Quarto deck does **not** meet this, even with `embed-resources`; the setup below does.

All reveal.js features and their Quarto syntax, with what was tested: `references/quarto-revealjs-guide.md`.
The author's talk conventions (words, notes, citations, backup slides): `references/style.md`;
read it before writing slides when the deck is the author's (Nathaniel Starkman's) own talk. Template files: `assets/`.

**Never open a visible browser window.** Every script here runs headless (Playwright); to look at a
deck use an embedded browser pane or a headless script, never a Chrome window or `open`.

## Set up a deck folder (once)

0. `git init` the folder on day one (the template's `.gitignore` keeps out `_output/`, `_share/`,
   `.venv/`; add any cloned data repository to it). Commit as you go; delete figures no slide uses
   any more (one talk's folder grew to 319 MB).
1. Copy everything in `assets/` into the folder: `_quarto.yml`, `_quarto-share.yml`, `.gitignore`,
   `_deck/`, `_extensions/` and the scripts.
2. Add the libraries the header loads (they are inlined into every deck at render time):
   - `_vendor/mathjax/tex-svg-full.js`: MathJax **3.2.2**, file `es5/tex-svg-full.js` from the
     `mathjax` npm package or the MathJax GitHub repository at tag `3.2.2`. The full build includes
     every TeX extension, so nothing is fetched later. (MathJax 4's SVG output loads font data at
     runtime; avoid it here.)
   - `_vendor/plotly/plotly.min.js`: copy it from the Python plotly package,
     `<site-packages>/plotly/package_data/plotly.min.js`, so the deck matches the Python version.

   ```bash
   mkdir -p _vendor/mathjax _vendor/plotly
   curl -fsSL -o _vendor/mathjax/tex-svg-full.js https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mathjax@3.2.2/es5/tex-svg-full.js
   cp "$(python -c 'import plotly, pathlib; print(pathlib.Path(plotly.__file__).parent / "package_data/plotly.min.js")')" _vendor/plotly/
   ```

   The header puts plotly.js (about 4.6 MB) into **every** deck. If no deck in the folder has
   Plotly figures, delete its `plotly.min.js` line from `_deck/header.html` and skip the copy.
3. Put the decks at the top of the folder: the header's `_vendor/` paths are relative to the deck.
   Each deck's front matter needs only its own settings, and must not set `embed-resources` or
   output options: front matter overrides `_quarto.yml`, profiles and `quarto render -M`, so a
   build could no longer change them. Put `jupyter: python3` here, not in
   `_quarto.yml`: there it was observed to be ignored, and Quarto picked another installed kernel.
   ````markdown
   ---
   title: "My talk"
   jupyter: python3
   ---

   {{< include _deck/setup.qmd >}}
   ````
   Include `_deck/setup.qmd` only in decks with Python Plotly cells.
4. `quarto render` renders every deck in the folder to `_output/`. The rendered decks are
   self-contained; `_vendor/` and `_deck/` are needed only to render.

Why each piece exists (all observed, not theoretical):

- reveal.js's math plugin always appends a MathJax `<script>`; by default from a CDN, even on decks
  without math. `_quarto.yml` points it at `about:blank`, and the header loads MathJax itself.
- `html-math-method: katex` is never embedded: offline the math is raw TeX.
- Every Plotly figure from plotly.py carries its own CDN MathJax `<script>` (a reduced build that
  cannot load extensions) and, in connected mode, an `import` of plotly.js from its CDN. Quarto inlines
  the first at render time, so a deck *with* a Plotly figure shows math that a deck *without* one
  does not. `_deck/setup.qmd` replaces the renderer with one that emits bare divs.

## Write slides

| Want | Write |
|---|---|
| Slide / section | `## Title {#id}` / `# Section` (with `navigation-mode: vertical`, sections become columns) |
| Speaker notes | `::: {.notes}` … `:::`; press **S** for the speaker view (works offline) |
| Step-by-step | `::: {.fragment .fade-up}`, `[word]{.fragment .highlight-red}`, `fragment-index=2`, `::: {.incremental}` |
| Step inside an equation | `\class{fragment}{…}` in TeX (needs the header script) |
| Code walk-through | ```` ```{.python code-line-numbers="\|1\|2-3"} ```` |
| Morph between slides | `{auto-animate="true"}` on both slides; same `data-id` on the element |
| Transition | YAML `transition: slide`; per slide `{transition="zoom"}` |
| Background | `{background-color=…}`, `background-gradient`, `background-image`, `background-video`, `background-iframe` |
| Layout | `.r-stack`, `.r-fit-text`, `.r-stretch`, `::: {.absolute top=… left=…}`, `:::: {.columns}` |
| Video / image zoom | `{{< video clip.mp4 >}}`; YAML `lightbox: true` + `![](img.png){.lightbox}` |
| Link to a slide | `[text](#id)`, **not** `#/id` (Quarto rewrites it to `#//id`) |
| Backup slides | `{visibility="uncounted"}`; drafts `{visibility="hidden"}` |
| JavaScript | a ```` ```{=html} ```` block with `<script>`; use `Reveal` after `window` `load` |
| Cite a paper | `{{< paper url="https://doi.org/…" who="Name et al." year="2021" title="…" >}}`; top right of a result slide: add `corner="true"` |
| Bibliography slide | `python bibliography.py <collection-key>` → `_bibliography.qmd`; `## References {.bibliography visibility="uncounted"}` then `{{< include _bibliography.qmd >}}` |
| Skip a build-up | press **]** (last step of the slide; again: next slide), from `_deck/skip-steps.html` |

The table escapes `|` as `\|`; in a deck write `code-line-numbers="|1|2-3"`.

Fragments must not change any heights: reserve the space and fade in; slides that build up one
figure keep an identical base-figure box and only add layers (guide, "Animations that do not jump").
`bibliography.py` reads the Zotero app's local API (enable it in Zotero's Advanced settings).

Everything else (themes, auto-slide, scroll view, keyboard, events, postMessage, plugins,
chalkboard, multiplex): `references/quarto-revealjs-guide.md`.

## Embed an interactive app (single-file HTML, e.g. a figpress-apps build)

Copy the app's single-file HTML into `apps/`. Inline on a slide (inlined into the deck, so still one
file):

```markdown
## The explorer

![](apps/explorer.png){.print-only .r-stretch}

::: {.r-stretch .print-hide style="position:relative; overflow:hidden;"}
<iframe src="apps/explorer.html" style="position:absolute; top:0; left:0; width:200%; height:200%;
  max-width:none; max-height:none; border:0; transform:scale(0.5); transform-origin:0 0;"></iframe>
:::
```

- 2× size scaled by 0.5 gives the app room for its wide layout; `max-width/max-height: none`
  undoes reveal.js's 95% cap on iframes.
- Full slide instead: `## {background-iframe="apps/explorer.html" background-interactive="true"}`.
  Quarto leaves a background iframe as a path; `python inline_apps.py _output/talk.html` (from the deck
  folder, or `--root <folder>`) puts the app inside the deck as base64 and serves it from a `blob:` URL at load. A `data:`
  URL is not enough: in the talk this came from, a real app stayed blank there (opaque origin;
  observed, not reproduced by the test, whose stand-in app runs either way). The same step swaps
  `<object data="file">`, which pandoc never inlines, for a `data:` URI.
- Match the deck's theme: an app that follows system dark mode must be pinned in its copy, e.g.
  `<html lang="en" data-theme="light">`. The deck cannot script into an inlined (`data:`) iframe, and
  Chrome does not pass an iframe's CSS `color-scheme` into the page.
- A live app does not reliably make it into the PDF: a 2D-canvas app in an inline iframe printed, the
  same app as a background iframe printed blank (observed by hand with `make_pdf.py`; WebGL untested). Give each app a `.print-only` still
  (a screenshot of it).
- A click into the app takes the keyboard; the header script gives it back so arrow keys still
  change slides.

## Check offline, then print

The scripts need `pip install playwright` and Google Chrome or Playwright's own browsers
(`python -m playwright install chromium webkit`). They run headless and block the network.

```bash
python inline_apps.py _output/my-talk.html    # background-iframe apps and <object> files inside
python check_offline.py _output/*.html        # network requests, missing files, errors, raw TeX
python check_overflow.py _output/*.html       # anything past the slide edge, in slide coordinates
python check_offline.py --webkit _output/*.html && python check_overflow.py --webkit _output/*.html
python make_pdf.py _output/my-talk.html       # -> _output/my-talk.pdf, notes on their own pages
```

`check_overflow.py` measures each slide with all fragments shown and names each element outside
the slide box with its position; it ignores notes, SVG internals, MathJax internals (struts,
assistive MathML) and content inside a clipping container. `--webkit` is Safari's engine; CSS path
animation and file-loaded CSS masks failed in Safari during a talk (guide, "Safari and WebKit").

A deck passes when it makes **no** network requests, misses no local file (a background video or
background-iframe app not shipped beside it), has no page errors and no raw TeX. "It rendered" is
not evidence: on a machine with internet a broken deck looks fine. `check_offline.py` allows the
math plugin's `about:blank` request, which loads nothing by design.
Then step through the deck once in the browser (S for notes, the app slides, fragments), and look at
the PDF: fragment steps are separate pages, live content shows its still.

`make_pdf.py` is reveal.js's own PDF route (`?print-pdf`) automated; Chrome's
`--headless --print-to-pdf` gives a blank page. Do not set `show-notes` in YAML: it shows the notes to
the audience. The script turns them on only for the PDF.

## A shareable copy

```bash
quarto render my-talk.qmd --profile share                    # _quarto-share.yml: output in _share/
python inline_apps.py --strip-notes _share/my-talk.html      # one file, no speaker notes
```

The archive build in `_output/` keeps the notes; the shared copy drops every `<aside class="notes">`.
The profile works only while the deck's front matter leaves `embed-resources` and output options
alone (front matter wins over profiles and `-M`).

## Gotchas

- Quarto 1.11.9 bundles reveal.js **5.1.0**: reveal's own lightbox (5.2+) and 6.x features are absent.
  Check `share/formats/revealjs/reveal/dist/reveal.js` in the Quarto install for the version.
- Preview links (`preview-link="true"`) only work for `http`/`www` URLs; a local file navigates away.
  Use `onclick="Reveal.showPreview(this.href); return false;"`.
- `.navigate-next` and friends: put them on a `<button>`; `<a href="#">` jumps to the title slide.
- YAML `keyboard:` takes only `true`/`false`: custom keys via `Reveal.addKeyBinding()`. postMessage
  replies need `Reveal.configure({postMessageEvents: true})`; no YAML option.
- Chalkboard refuses `embed-resources` (render that deck as a folder); multiplex needs a hosted server.
- Background video and parallax images stay relative paths: ship them. Background iframes too,
  until `inline_apps.py` runs.
- A fragment `.grow` on a full-width block scales off the left edge; put it on a span.
- Re-rendering while the deck is open over HTTP: reload without cache (Shift-Cmd-R) to see changes
  in background iframes.

name: submit-hybrid-compute
description: Split a research project between a local machine and MIT's subMIT cluster (submit.mit.edu, the physics department's login pool and Slurm cluster), with code and results kept in sync through a private git repo. Light work (editing, plotting, quick checks) stays local; heavy compute runs as Slurm jobs on the submit partition. Use when the user mentions subMIT, submit.mit.edu, the submit or tier3 partitions, /work/submit or /ceph/submit, sbatch/squeue on subMIT, moving runs there from a laptop or from Engaging, syncing results back, or a project that already has this setup (a clone under /work/submit, a deploy key, slurm/ scripts).
---

# Local ↔ subMIT hybrid compute, synced through a private git repo

One repo, two working copies:

```
local machine                          GitHub (private repo)                 subMIT (clone in /work/submit/<kerb>)
edit, commit, push   ───────────────▶  origin  ◀───── pull --rebase (deploy key) ─────  login node: git pull, uv sync, sbatch
pull --rebase, plot  ◀───────────────          ◀──── push_results.sh (figures, small arrays) ── after jobs finish
```

- **Code** is written locally, committed and pushed. The cluster only pulls.
- **Results** that are small and cheap to regenerate (figures, small `.npz`/`.json`, result tables) are committed *on the cluster* by `push_results.sh` and pulled locally.
- **Big things** (raw outputs, caches, `.venv`, Slurm logs) never go in git. Move them with `rsync` only when needed.
- **Heavy compute only in Slurm jobs.** Locally: editing, plotting, reading results, checks that take seconds.

For a one-off run of an existing project (no deploy key yet), `rsync` the working tree to `/work/submit/<kerb>/<project>` instead of cloning; the rest of this file still applies.

Read `setup.md` (next to this file) for the one-time setup. The rest of this file is the daily workflow and the rules.

## Connecting (SSH key only, no Duo)

subMIT logs in with an SSH key that the user uploaded to the submit portal (https://submit-portal.mit.edu, behind Touchstone). There is no Duo prompt, so no ControlMaster or reconnect helper is needed: every call is a fresh connection.

- Run everything as `ssh -o BatchMode=yes <alias> '<cmd>'` (`<alias>` is the `~/.ssh/config` host, e.g. `submit`). `BatchMode` makes a refused key fail fast instead of prompting.
- `submit.mit.edu` is a **round-robin of login nodes** (submit01…submit08 and so on). Two calls can land on different machines. `/home`, `/work` and `/ceph` are shared, so files are the same everywhere, but processes are not: a `nohup` or `screen` you started on one call may not be on the next login node. Use Slurm for anything long-running, never a background process on a login node.
- If the key is refused, stop and ask the user. Don't retry in a loop. Read the error first:
  - `sign_and_send_pubkey: signing failed ... communication with agent failed` then `Permission denied (publickey)`: the local SSH agent (1Password) is locked or asleep. Ask the user to unlock it.
  - A plain `Permission denied (publickey)` with no agent error: the key isn't on the portal (anymore). The user re-uploads it.

The key opens a full shell on the user's account. Treat every command as if the user typed it, and keep to the rules below even when nothing prompts.

Never touch `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` on the cluster: the portal manages keys.

## Rules

- **Login nodes are shared and busy** (load ~50 is normal). Allowed there: `git`, `uv sync` (installs), `rsync`, `sbatch`/`squeue`/`sacct`/`scancel`, reading logs, short tests (seconds to a couple of minutes). Anything longer goes in a Slurm job. subMIT's guide sets ~15 minutes as the line; stay well under it.
- **Storage:** home is only **10 GB**. Put the clone, `.venv` and the uv cache in `/work/submit/<kerb>` (100 GB). Large data goes in `/ceph/submit/data/user/<k>/<kerb>` (1 TB, large files only: no 100k+ small files). See `setup.md`.
- **Partitions:** `submit` for CPU work (6 days max). `tier3` has old CPUs **without AVX2** (mostly without AVX): JAX, standard TensorFlow and many optimized wheels die there with `Illegal instruction`. Never send such jobs to `tier3` or to `--partition=submit,tier3`. GPUs: `submit-gpu` (2 days), `submit-gpu-express` (1 h).
- **Always pass `--time`.** Without it a job gets the 12 h default, which both kills long runs and hides short ones from backfill.
- **Ask the user before:**
  - jobs beyond the project's agreed size, for example > 1 day, more than ~20 array tasks or > 32 CPUs per task (agree the thresholds per project);
  - GPU jobs, unless agreed;
  - deleting anything on the cluster;
  - emailing submit-help@mit.edu or asking for more quota (the user does that);
  - changing pinned dependencies.
- **Keep the repo private.** Never commit secrets, keys or tokens. `push_results.sh` commits every `.json` in an experiment folder, so no credentials go in those folders, and job logs print only named switches, never the whole environment.
- **Commit signing:** if a commit fails because the signing agent is locked (1Password's SSH agent), ask the user to unlock 1Password. Never bypass signing.
- **If something breaks, stop and report.** Don't quietly fall back to running locally or to a different dependency source.

## The daily loop

1. **Local:** edit → commit → push.
2. **Cluster:** update the clone, then **verify the code arrived** before submitting:
   ```bash
   ssh -o BatchMode=yes <alias> 'cd <cluster-repo> && git pull -q --rebase --autostash && git log --oneline -1 && grep -c "<a symbol you just added>" <file>'
   ```
   Run `uv sync --frozen` only if the lockfile changed.
   *Why verify:* if the local commit silently failed (e.g. signing), the cluster runs the old code and you only find out hours later.
3. **Submit** with `sbatch`, usually the generic array script `scripts/run_modes.sh` (one mode per task). Give jobs **descriptive names**: they're how you watch them.
4. **Watch** by job name, not by a list of IDs (see Monitoring).
5. **Collect:** on the login node, `scripts/push_results.sh "<what these results are>"` commits figures and small arrays and pushes.
6. **Local:** check what the cluster pushed, then pull:
   ```bash
   git fetch -q && git log --stat HEAD..@{u}
   ```
   Cluster commits should touch only result files in experiment folders. If one changes code, scripts or config, stop and tell the user before pulling: the deploy key may be misused. Then `git pull --rebase`, plot, analyse and write notes.

## Submitting jobs well

- **Pilot first, with a short limit.** A few-minute job on the real code (`-t 00:08:00`) gives the per-step time and memory; size the real jobs from it. Run it at two CPU counts in parallel and compare the step times: they often land on the same node, which makes the comparison clean. `seff <jobid>` gives CPU efficiency and peak memory even for a pilot killed at its time limit.
  - Example (a JAX orbit integration): 4 CPUs → 10.4 s/step at 57% CPU efficiency; 8 CPUs → 9.4 s/step at 40%. Doubling the CPUs bought 10% for twice the billing, so 4 it is. JAX's CPU backend often uses only 2–3 cores.
  - Node speed varies between nodes (and between clusters: the same step took 5.8 s on an Engaging node). Set `--time` from the slowest pilot plus a wide margin; the 6-day partition limit leaves room.
- **Split long checkpointed runs into an array.** If a script already loops over independent chunks and checkpoints each one, run one chunk per array task through a small runner that narrows the loop (and skips the final assembly), then one dependent job that runs the unmodified script and reuses every checkpoint. The pipeline's own script stays untouched. The runner forwards the script's arguments verbatim and takes its chunk from `SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID`, never from a rewritten argv: in one run, a runner that reset `sys.argv` silently computed the default grid instead of the requested one. Printing the configuration (below) catches this on the first lines.
- **Settings via environment, passed with `--export=ALL,KEY=val,...`.** `--export` **splits on commas**, so never put a comma inside a value: `KAPPAS=8,4,2,1` arrives as `KAPPAS=8`. Use another separator (`8:4:2:1`).
- **Every switch that changes results must appear in the output filename.** Two jobs that differ only in an env var otherwise overwrite each other's output.
- **Print the full configuration on the first lines of each job log**, and check the first lines of one task before trusting a whole batch.
- **Memory is a consumable resource on subMIT**, like CPUs: a job holding a node's memory blocks that node even if its CPUs sit idle. Request from history (`seff <jobid>` or `sacct -o MaxRSS`) plus a cushion. Most nodes have 64–128 GB.
- **Before comparing a rerun with a cached result, check that the cache came from the same code and inputs** (grid sizes, shapes, file dates against the git log). A cache that build tools copy without hashing inputs can outlive the code that made it. Compare on matching keys (e.g. parameter pairs), not on array positions.
- **Chain dependent steps:** `sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid> ...`. Have the upstream step exit non-zero if its result is unusable; `afterok` only sees the exit code.
- **Jobs read the code when they *start*, not when you submit.** Pulling new code on the cluster changes what *queued* jobs will run. Pull only when the change is backward compatible for queued jobs, or wait until they've started.
- **Logs:** `#SBATCH -o slurm/logs/%x-%j.out` (arrays: `%x-%A_%a.out`). The directory must exist before `sbatch`.
- **Thread counts:** inside a job, `os.cpu_count()` reports the whole node. Pin threads (`OMP_NUM_THREADS`, `XLA_FLAGS`, etc.) to `$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK` if oversubscription shows up.
- **Tools in `~/.local/bin` (e.g. `uv`) aren't on the batch `PATH`.** Call them by full path in job scripts, and export `UV_CACHE_DIR` to `/work` (see `setup.md`).

## Fair share

subMIT uses multifactor priority with fair share as the largest weight (check `scontrol show config | grep ^Priority`; at the time of writing FairShare 10000, JobSize 2000, Partition 1000, Age 500, with a 7-day decay half-life). Billing is CPUs × elapsed time. The cluster is shared by the whole department, so the same discipline as on any fair-share cluster applies:

- **Ask what question the batch answers**, and run the smallest set of jobs that answers it. Screen with one seed or a pilot, then expand only the informative variants. Skip outputs that already exist.
- **Right-size:** `-c` only what the code uses (compare `sacct -o Elapsed,TotalCPU,AllocCPUS` or `seff`), `-t` from past runs plus a margin, `--mem` from MaxRSS plus a cushion. Short accurate limits backfill into idle gaps.
- **The partition is often full.** Even with top fair share, array tasks can wait as `(Resources)`: one evening, 28 of 29 `submit` nodes were allocated and over 1000 jobs were pending, so 2 of 8 tasks started at once and the rest queued. Plan for wall time beyond the run time, and check with `sinfo -p submit -o "%D %T"` and `squeue --me --start`.
- `sshare -l -u $USER` shows `LevelFS = share / usage` (below 1: over your share); `sprio -j <id>` breaks down one pending job.
- **Cancel jobs as soon as they stop being informative.** Ask first if the user started them.
- **Pack small runs that share setup into one job**, so imports and JIT compilation are paid once.

## Monitoring

Use `scripts/watch_jobs.sh <name-regex>` (or the same loop inline) as a background task:
- **Match jobs by name with `squeue --me -h -o %j | grep -cE '<regex>'`.** `squeue -j id1,id2,...` prints nothing when one ID is invalid or finished, which looks like "all done".
- **Treat an ssh failure as a failure, not as "0 jobs left".**
- **An overnight watcher dies when 1Password auto-locks** (each check is a fresh connection, and a locked agent refuses to sign). The jobs keep running; only the watcher stops. Tell the user before a long watch, so they can lengthen 1Password's auto-lock or accept checking in by hand after unlocking.
- Sleep 5–20 minutes between checks. When the jobs disappear, print the result lines from the logs.

Useful checks:
```bash
squeue --me -o "%i %j %T %M %l %R"      # state, elapsed, limit, reason or node
sacct -X -n -S <date> -o JobID%14,JobName%22,State%12,Elapsed
seff <jobid>                            # CPU and memory efficiency of a finished job
srun --jobid=<jobid> --overlap --pty bash   # a shell on a running job's node (user only; interactive)
```

## Bookkeeping

- Keep a running notes file in the repo (decisions, findings, job IDs, what each result means) and commit it often in small logical commits.
- Keep a cluster notes file for setup facts and gotchas, and append new ones.
- Each experiment gets its own folder (`NN_short_name/`) with a runnable script, so `push_results.sh` can glob results by folder.
- At the end of the project phase, revoke the deploy key and clean up `/work` and `/ceph`: storage there is yours to keep tidy.

name: syw-adopt-overleaf
description: Runbook for moving an existing paper (a live Overleaf project, often with co-authors, plus a private git repository) into a fresh showyourwork (SYW) repository without losing or silently changing anything. Backs up first, rebuilds figures and numbers from code and compares the new PDF with the old one, keeps the old git history private, and stops for the author's yes before every irreversible step. Use this whenever the user wants to "adopt", "migrate", "convert" or "move" a paper to showyourwork, put an existing Overleaf paper under SYW, or make an older paper reproducible, even if they only say "set up showyourwork for this paper". Afterwards the paper is ready for syw-overleaf-dropbox (daily work) and syw-site init (paper site).
---

# Moving an existing Overleaf paper into showyourwork

The paper is real, often submitted, and other people edit it. Nothing may be lost, no number
may change silently, and the old repository's history must never become public. So the
migration is a runbook with checkpoints: the agent prepares, the author decides.

**The result:** a new private repository `paper-<slug>` whose history starts at
`[showyourwork] first commit`; the *same* Overleaf project (same co-authors, links and history)
with the text renamed to SYW's defaults `ms.tex` / `bib.bib`; figures and numbers built by code;
the old repository archived, untouched otherwise.

## Hard rules

- **⛔ gates.** Every step marked ⛔ below waits for the author's explicit yes in chat. Record
  each answer in `MIGRATION.md` (one line: phase, what was shown, answer, date).
- **The author acts, the agent prepares**: sending the co-author freeze message, setting
  Overleaf's main document, setting repository secrets, changing repository visibility.
- **Never `showyourwork setup --overleaf=<id>`** on an existing project: that code path is for an
  empty project and SYW also ships a function that wipes one. Set up without `--overleaf`; the
  `overleaf:` section is added by hand in phase 6.
- **The new repository never fetches from the old one** (no `git remote add old`, no
  `git fetch <bundle>`). Text comes from the Overleaf clone, code is copied as files.
- **Tokens** are read inline (`op read`) on the one command that needs them, never printed,
  written, logged or put in a URL. Redact `access_token=` when reading SYW logs.
- **Signing:** never bypass commit signing. If signing fails, ask the author to unlock 1Password.
- **Private until arXiv:** the repository is created private; any docs site stays local.
- **Never compile in the Dropbox mirror:** aux files there sync into the co-authors' project.
  Compile a temporary copy.
- Touch nothing else of the author's: other repositories, branches, worktrees, uncommitted work.

## Before starting

Find, and write into `MIGRATION.md` → Sources: the old repository (local clone and
`owner/name`), the Dropbox mirror (`~/Library/CloudStorage/Dropbox/Apps/Overleaf/<Project>/`),
the Overleaf project id (Overleaf → Menu → Git, or the project URL), the 1Password reference of
the Overleaf git token, and the SYW version to use (ask; e.g. a development install). Propose a
slug from the title (short, lowercase, hyphens) and get the author's confirmation of
`paper-<slug>`.

## Phases

### 0. Survey (read-only)

1. Read the paper's build: main file, bibliography, class/bst files, preamble packages,
   submodules, any `\variable`-like macro, `make variables` / `variables.yml`, figure scripts,
   data locations, lockfiles.
2. Compile the current Overleaf text **in a temporary copy of the mirror** (latexmk) — or, if the
   local toolchain cannot build it, ask the author to download Overleaf's compiled PDF. That PDF
   is `baseline.pdf`.
3. Inventory every Overleaf file into `inventory.tsv` (class 1–4, see `references/mapping.md`),
   using the post-rename names. Check that every file in the Overleaf project appears exactly
   once.

### 1. Backup ⛔

```sh
scripts/backup.sh --repo <old clone> --mirror "<mirror>" --overleaf-id <id> \
    --op-ref 'op://<vault>/<item>/credential' --baseline baseline.pdf [--github <owner/name>] [--dest <backups root>]
```

`--github` is needed when the old repository has no `origin` (for example when it *is* the
Dropbox mirror folder); if GitHub holds a different history (Overleaf's own GitHub sync), it is
bundled too, as `github.bundle`.

Writes `<dest>/<old-repo>-<YYYY-MM-DD>/` (`--dest` defaults to `~/backups`) (refuses Dropbox/iCloud and an
existing folder) with `repo.bundle`, `mirror.tar.gz`, `overleaf/` (clone with Overleaf's
history), `baseline.pdf`, `secrets.txt` (names only) and a `MIGRATION.md` from
`references/migration-template.md`; every part verified. Move `inventory.tsv` there.
⛔ Show the `ok` lines; the author confirms before anything changes.

### 2. Freeze Overleaf

Draft a short message asking co-authors not to edit until the migration is done (expected
duration, who to contact). The author sends it. If the Overleaf project is linked to a GitHub
repository through Overleaf's own GitHub integration (Menu → GitHub), note it: Overleaf cannot
unlink a single project, so from now on nobody uses that menu, and phase 8 retires the repository.
Record Overleaf's HEAD (from the backup clone) in `MIGRATION.md` → Freeze.

### 3. Build the SYW layout locally

In a new folder `<parent>/paper-<slug>/` (a new repository; nothing from the old one's `.git`):

1. `showyourwork setup` (no `--overleaf`) with the agreed SYW version → commit 1,
   `[showyourwork] first commit`.
2. Place files per the inventory (`references/mapping.md`): text from **the backup's Overleaf
   clone** under its new names `src/tex/ms.tex`, `src/tex/bib.bib` (and `\bibliography{bib}`);
   class-3 files into `src/tex/`; code to `src/scripts/`, data to `src/data/`; Snakefile rules for
   every figure and cited number. Keep every `ms.tex` change in an exact-match edit script in the
   backup folder (`ms_edits.py`): phase 6 replays it on Overleaf so the first pull is
   byte-identical. The usual edits, and the other first-build failures, are in
   `references/lessons.md`.
2. Run the old tests. Point pytest's `testpaths` at the package, never at `src/scripts`:
   importing a figure script runs it. Commit 2, `[showyourwork] migrate paper sources`. The
   prefix matters: SYW's pull refuses to overwrite a file whose last commit is not a
   `[showyourwork]` commit.
3. `showyourwork.yml` has **no `overleaf:` section yet**. Draft the push/pull lists in
   `MIGRATION.md` and run `scripts/check_lists.py <draft> inventory.tsv` until `ok`. Its
   `deleted:` lines are the class-4 files the first push removes from Overleaf (a pushed folder
   replaces the whole Overleaf folder); they are approved at the dry run.

### 4. Build and compare ⛔

Build locally (Zenodo token inline if the paper caches on Zenodo). Then:

```sh
scripts/pdf_diff.py baseline.pdf ms.pdf --out pdf-diff/
```

Show every section that differs (`numbers` first, then `images` with the PNGs, then `text`,
`pages`). For each difference: find the cause (code, data, a hand-edited figure, a font), fix
what is a migration error, and leave what the author accepts. Repeat 3–4. ⛔ The author accepts
the remaining differences, one by one; record them in `MIGRATION.md` → PDF differences.

SYW compiles with tectonic and Overleaf with pdflatex, so `ms.pdf` differs from the baseline
everywhere (hyphenation, line numbers, the SYW stamp) and that diff hides real changes. Compare
the parts instead: each regenerated figure against the old one (`pdf_diff.py`), every generated
number file byte for byte, and the migrated `src/tex/` compiled with pdflatex in a temporary
copy against the baseline (expect only `\today`). Then show the author the two PDFs side by side,
page by page: a figure moving to another page is layout work they will want to know about.

### 5. Create the new repository ⛔

**If any rule is `cache: True`, seed the Zenodo cache before `main` reaches GitHub.** With no
Sandbox DOI in `zenodo.yml`, CI does not treat those rules as cached and runs them (a 21-hour
rule once ran on a runner until cancelled). ⛔ With the author's yes, `showyourwork cache create`
(token inline) makes a private Sandbox draft and writes its DOI. To upload existing results
instead of recomputing:

1. Read the rule's cache key without letting any script run: build once with
   `UV_CONFIG_FILE=/nonexistent` (every `uv run` then exits at once; the key is not affected) and
   take the hash from `Searching for file \`<rule>\` with hash \`<key>\`` in
   `.showyourwork/logs/showyourwork.log`.
2. Copy the results to `.showyourwork/cache/<key>` (a folder for a directory output, the file
   plus its extension otherwise).
3. Build normally (with any `local_cache` entry for that rule off for this one build): SYW restores
   from the local cache and uploads to the draft. The draft's notes list each rule's key.

Then ⛔ `gh repo create <owner>/paper-<slug> --private --source . --push`. The author sets the
secrets (`OVERLEAF_TOKEN`, and `SANDBOX_TOKEN`/`ZENODO_TOKEN` if used) in the GitHub UI or with
`op read … | gh secret set NAME -R <owner>/paper-<slug>` run themselves. Watch the first CI run:
it should restore cached rules (`Restoring from Zenodo Sandbox cache`), not run them. The old
repository is not touched.

### 6. Rename, then first sync

Still frozen; compare Overleaf's HEAD with the one recorded at the freeze, and stop to reconcile
if a co-author edited.

1. ⛔ In a fresh Overleaf clone (credential helper as in `backup.sh`, in a temporary folder):
   `git mv main.tex ms.tex`, `git mv main.bib bib.bib`, run `ms_edits.py ms.tex`, add
   `showyourwork.sty` (the edited `ms.tex` loads it, so Overleaf cannot compile without it).
   `cmp` `ms.tex`/`bib.bib` with `src/tex/`: byte-identical. Show the diff, commit, push.
2. ⛔ The author sets Overleaf **Menu → Main document** to `ms.tex`.
3. The author recompiles in Overleaf and downloads the PDF; `pdf_diff.py baseline.pdf <it>`
   shows only `\today` (and, if Overleaf's pdfTeX differs from the local one, sub-pixel
   anti-aliasing in figures; zoom in to confirm).
4. **Dry run.** SYW pulls and pushes only on branch `main`, and has no dry-run flag. So, on a
   branch `overleaf-sync` (not `main`): add the `overleaf:` section (`id`,
   `gh_actions_sync: true`, the checked lists) and commit it, **unpushed**. Simulate the push on
   a copy of a fresh Overleaf clone: for each `push` entry, delete the Overleaf folder and copy
   `src/tex/<entry>` in its place (files: copy over); `git add -A; git status --short`. Show the
   author:
   - every write and **every deletion**, with where each deleted file lives afterwards (the
     repository by content hash, regenerated by a rule, or the backup only). Files only in the
     backup are the author's call: keep them in the repository (gitignored if private) or not;
   - `ms.tex`/`bib.bib` in the clone byte-identical to `src/tex/`;
   - `check_lists.py showyourwork.yml inventory.tsv` → `ok`, its `deleted:` count matching.
   ⛔ The author approves.
5. Merge to `main`. Read each token into a variable and check it is non-empty first (a timed-out
   `op read` gives an empty string and SYW then skips the sync quietly). Run the full SYW build
   (pull, build, push). SYW pushes from an `onsuccess` handler that Snakemake skips when there is
   nothing to do: if the log has no `Pushing changes to Overleaf`, delete `ms.pdf` and build
   again. Compare Overleaf's new commit with the dry run (same files, same change types; pushed
   figures identical to the old ones). Push to GitHub.
6. The first CI run on `main` syncs Overleaf with **CI's** build. Compare every figure it pushed
   with the local one: `pdfinfo` page size, then `pdf_diff.py`. Two CI-only failures
   have come up here (cached outputs in `src/tex/` crashing the cache restore; a figure whose size depended on
   the matplotlib backend); both are in `references/lessons.md`.

### 7. Prune ⛔

List every file in a fresh Overleaf clone that the sync lists do not cover, with its class and
its identical copy in the repository, if any. ⛔ The author approves the list (keeping a file is
an answer). Delete them in the clone, compile that exact tree with pdflatex in a temporary copy
(it must still build), then commit and push. Overleaf's git access does not export hidden
folders (`.vscode/`, `.figure-baseline/`): the author deletes those in Overleaf's file tree.
The author recompiles in Overleaf and tells co-authors the freeze is over.

The Dropbox mirror may still hold the old checkout (`.git`, `.venv`, notes) next to Overleaf's
files. ⛔ With the author's choice for it, delete only files whose content is in
`mirror.tar.gz`; afterwards the mirror's file set must equal Overleaf's exactly.

### 8. Hand off ⛔

1. `sh <syw-overleaf-dropbox>/scripts/check_build.sh "<mirror>" build.log` in the new repository:
   push found, no missing variables, every figure (subfolders too) same as the mirror. With
   `gh_actions_sync`, a figure CI rebuilt differs in bytes from the local one; compare content.
2. Check the old GitHub repository against the backup before retiring it: a fresh
   `git clone --mirror` has the same refs as the bundle; list what lives only on GitHub (issues,
   PRs and comments, releases, wiki, secrets, Actions artifacts); and look up every blob in its
   history (`git rev-list --objects --all`) in the new repository, `repo.bundle`, the Overleaf
   backup, `mirror.tar.gz` and any submodule's repository. Report the blobs found only on GitHub.
   ⛔ Then archive (`gh repo archive <owner>/<old> --yes`) or, if the author asks, delete
   (`gh repo delete`; needs `gh auth refresh -h github.com -s delete_repo`, run by the author).
   Overleaf's GitHub link cannot be removed per project; an archived or deleted repository makes
   any accidental push from Overleaf's GitHub menu fail.
3. Point the author to `syw-overleaf-dropbox` for daily work and `syw-site init` for a paper site.
4. New gotchas go into `references/lessons.md`.

## Before the repository is ever made public

The author decides when (typically at arXiv). First run:

```sh
scripts/public_check.sh <new repo> <backup>/repo.bundle <backup>/inventory.tsv
```

Run it once per bundle (`repo.bundle`, and `github.bundle` if there is one). It fails on any
commit shared with the old repository, a token-like string anywhere in history,
or a class-4 file marked `private` ever committed. Identical file contents are fine.

## If something goes wrong

Every phase has restore steps in `references/rollback.md`. In short: the old repository is
unchanged until phase 8; Overleaf can be restored from the backup clone or Overleaf's history;
the new repository and folder can be deleted until the author has used them.

## Files

- `references/mapping.md` — the four classes, rules, inventory format, a worked example.
- `references/rollback.md` — restore commands per phase.
- `references/lessons.md` — what went wrong in earlier migrations, and why.
- `references/migration-template.md` — the `MIGRATION.md` skeleton.
- `scripts/backup.sh`, `scripts/pdf_diff.py`, `scripts/check_lists.py`, `scripts/public_check.sh`
  — run each with no arguments for usage. `pdf_diff.py` needs poppler.
