## Redirects

Every URL changes in a restructure. Both extensions below emit meta-refresh HTML, which is a
workaround for static hosts; if you control the server (or use Netlify `_redirects`, Cloudflare
rules, or Read the Docs' redirect dashboard), do server-side 301s and treat the extension as a
belt-and-braces fallback.

### sphinxext-rediraffe — for in-project restructures, CI-enforceable

This is the right default here, because it can **fail the build when you move a file without
adding a redirect**.

```python
extensions += ["sphinxext.rediraffe"]
rediraffe_branch = "main"
rediraffe_redirects = "redirects.txt"
```

`docs/redirects.txt` — source filenames *with* extensions on both sides:

```
# comments start with '#'
getting-started.md          tutorials/installation.md
guides/authentication.md    how-to/authenticate.md
'design notes.md'           explanation/architecture.md
```

Builders:

```bash
sphinx-build -b rediraffecheckdiff docs docs/_build   # CI: fails if a moved file has no redirect
sphinx-build -b rediraffewritediff docs docs/_build   # adds renames automatically
```

`rediraffewritediff` only works with configuration files and cannot detect deleted files.
Rediraffe chains transitively (A→B, B→C implies A→C), which matters across successive
restructure increments.

### sphinx-reredirects — for wildcards and cross-domain moves

Source is a **docname** (no suffix); target is a URL matching the builder's output naming.

```python
extensions += ["sphinx_reredirects"]
redirects = {
    "getting-started":       "tutorials/installation.html",
    "guides/authentication": "../how-to/authenticate.html",
    "faq/*":                 "explanation/faq/$source.html",
    "*":                     "https://newdocs.example.com/$source.html",
}
```

Wildcards are `fnmatch` only (`*`, `?`, `[seq]`, `[!seq]`) — `**` has no special meaning. `$source`
is the matched docname and has no suffix, so append `.html` or `/`. With the `dirhtml` builder,
targets must be folders (`"install/"`). A source that already exists gets **overwritten** with
the redirect; wildcards only expand against existing documents, so explicitly list pages you
have `git mv`d away.

Its default template preserves the URL fragment via JavaScript, which matters a lot — deep links
into old pages carry anchors. Override with `redirect_html_template_file`.

### Canonical URLs

```python
html_baseurl = "https://docs.example.com/en/stable/"
```

Emits `<link rel="canonical">` on every page. Set it before the restructure ships, and update it
if the site itself moves.

---

## rst and md together

A mixed tree is normal during migration and fully supported.

```python
source_suffix = {".rst": "restructuredtext", ".md": "markdown"}
```

Cross-references resolve across the boundary — targets live in Sphinx's domain registries, not
in the parser — so `{ref}` from a `.md` page finds a label in a `.rst` page. That is what makes
incremental conversion safe.

Markdown inside rST:

```rst
.. include:: include.md
   :parser: myst_parser.sphinx_
```

Inside roles, use rST-style `` {role}`Text <target>` ``, not Markdown link syntax — some roles
hard-code the rST pattern.

**Move first, convert second, in separate commits.** A combined diff is unreviewable and
rediraffe's rename detection works on similarity. If the rST side uses
`sphinx.ext.autosectionlabel`, expect duplicate-label warnings during the mixed period, since
its slugs differ from `myst_heading_anchors`.

```python
extensions = [
    "myst_parser",
    "sphinx_design",
    "sphinx.ext.intersphinx",
    "sphinxext.rediraffe",
]

source_suffix = {".rst": "restructuredtext", ".md": "markdown"}
root_doc = "index"
exclude_patterns = ["_build", "**.ipynb_checkpoints"]

myst_enable_extensions = [
    "colon_fence", "deflist", "substitution", "fieldlist", "attrs_block", "linkify",
]
myst_heading_anchors = 3

intersphinx_mapping = {"python": ("https://docs.python.org/3", None)}

html_theme = "pydata_sphinx_theme"

}

## CI

```bash
python <skill-dir>/scripts/check_links.py docs/           # fast, pre-build, checks fragments too
sphinx-build -W --keep-going -b html docs docs/_build/html
sphinx-build -b rediraffecheckdiff docs docs/_build/redirects
sphinx-build -b linkcheck docs docs/_build/linkcheck
```

Run `check_links.py` first while editing: it works on a tree that does not build yet, and it
verifies `#fragment` targets against heading slugs and explicit anchors, which is where a
restructure breaks links most quietly. `redirects.txt` for rediraffe can be generated with
`scripts/make_redirect_stubs.py --emit rediraffe` from a two-column file of old and new *source
filenames* (`getting-started.md tutorials/installation.md`), not from the migration map's
redirect table: that holds URLs, and rediraffe rejects URL entries as broken redirects.

`-W` turns warnings into errors, which with `nitpicky = True` means a broken cross-mode
reference fails CI. That is what makes "link instead of duplicating" a discipline the project
can actually keep. `rediraffecheckdiff` is the guard that stops a moved page from losing its
inbound links. Note that linkcheck does not currently verify redirects to other pages within
the same documentation.

## Read this first: redirects

A Diátaxis restructure changes every URL, so settle redirects before any files move. Zensical
has a built-in `redirects` plugin (the `mkdocs-redirects` configuration, no install needed).
Older Zensical releases had none, so check the project's pinned version first. Paths are source
files relative to `docs_dir`, and you can map a single anchor of a page that was split:

```toml
[project.plugins.redirects.redirect_maps]
"getting-started.md" = "tutorials/installation.md"
"usage.md" = "how-to/schedule-runs.md"
"usage.md#flags" = "reference/cli.md#flags"
```

Each old page becomes a meta-refresh page that keeps the URL fragment. Anchors you did not map
go to the page-level target. No Markdown file may remain at the old path. The options:

1. **Host-level redirects** — Netlify `_redirects`, Cloudflare rules, nginx/Apache config,
   CloudFront functions. Best outcome: real 301s. Requires control of hosting.
2. **The `redirects` plugin** above: works anywhere, including GitHub Pages. Fill
   `redirect_maps` from the migration map's redirect table, as source filenames, not URLs.
3. **Generated meta-refresh stub pages** at the old paths, if the plugin cannot be used. Generate
   them from the migration map — do not hand-write them:

   ```bash
   python <skill-dir>/scripts/make_redirect_stubs.py \
       --map audit/migration-map.md --emit stubs --out redirects/ --url-style dirhtml
   ```

   The stubs preserve the URL fragment and route split-page anchors to different destinations,
   which is the part that goes wrong by hand. Copy the output into `site/` after each build.
4. **Keep URLs stable** — reorganize nav and rewrite content without moving files. This
   preserves links completely and still delivers most of the benefit, since the mode separation
   and the rewrites are where the value is. Consider it seriously for a public doc set with
   significant inbound traffic.

Whichever you choose, say so explicitly in the plan.

---

## Project shape

```
.
├─ docs/
│  ├─ index.md
│  ├─ tutorials/index.md
│  ├─ how-to/index.md
│  ├─ reference/index.md
│  └─ explanation/index.md
├─ overrides/            # optional theme custom_dir
└─ zensical.toml
```

`docs_dir` defaults to `docs`, `site_dir` to `site`. `docs_dir` cannot be `"."` (a stated
temporary limitation). `zensical new <dir>` scaffolds a project and refuses to overwrite
existing files.

Install with `pip install zensical` or `uv add --dev zensical` (Python ≥3.10). uv symlink mode
is unsupported.

---

## Configuration

`zensical.toml` (preferred) or `mkdocs.yml` / `mkdocs.yaml`. Resolution order is
`zensical.toml` → `mkdocs.yml` → `mkdocs.yaml`. All settings currently live under `[project]`
and sub-scopes; the docs warn that scopes will move as the schema matures, with automatic
refactorings promised.

```toml
[project]
site_name = "Toolkit"
site_url = "https://docs.example.com/"
site_description = "Documentation for Toolkit"
repo_url = "https://github.com/example/toolkit"
edit_uri = "edit/main/docs/"

nav = [
  { "Home" = "index.md" },
  { "Tutorials" = [
    "tutorials/index.md",
    { "Install and first run" = "tutorials/installation.md" },
    { "Your first pipeline" = "tutorials/first-pipeline.md" },
  ] },
  { "How-to guides" = [
    "how-to/index.md",
    { "How to authenticate" = "how-to/authenticate.md" },
  ] },
  { "Reference" = [
    "reference/index.md",
    { "CLI" = "reference/cli.md" },
    { "Configuration" = "reference/configuration.md" },
  ] },
  { "Explanation" = [
    "explanation/index.md",
    { "About the architecture" = "explanation/architecture.md" },
  ] },
]

[project.theme]
language = "en"
features = [
  "navigation.indexes",     # required for section landing pages
  "navigation.sections",
  "navigation.tabs",        # four modes as top-level tabs
  "navigation.path",        # breadcrumbs — helps readers know which mode they are in
  "navigation.top",
  "navigation.footer",
  "content.tabs.link",      # tab choice persists site-wide
  "content.code.copy",
  "content.code.annotate",
  "search.highlight",
]

[project.markdown_extensions]
admonition = {}
attr_list = {}
def_list = {}
md_in_html = {}
toc.permalink = true
pymdownx.details = {}
pymdownx.superfences = {}
pymdownx.tabbed.alternate_style = true
pymdownx.snippets = {}
```

TOML idioms to know: extension options use dotted keys (`pymdownx.highlight.anchor_linenums =
true`), an extension with no options is `name = {}`, and YAML `!!python/name:` tags become plain
strings.

`mkdocs.yml` settings **not** supported: `remote_branch`, `remote_name`, `exclude_docs`,
`draft_docs`, `not_in_nav`, `hooks`.

---

## Navigation

Navigation is generated from the folder structure by default; an explicit `nav` overrides it.
Paths are relative to `docs_dir`. Use an explicit `nav` for a Diátaxis site — mode order is
deliberate (tutorials first, explanation last) and alphabetical folder order will not give it
to you.

```toml
nav = [ "index.md", "about.md" ]                              # titles inferred from content
nav = [ { "Home" = "index.md" } ]                             # explicit title
nav = [ { "About" = [ "about/index.md", "about/team.md" ] } ] # nested section
nav = [ { "GitHub" = "https://github.com/example/toolkit" } ] # unresolvable string = URL
```

Useful theme features for a four-mode site: `navigation.tabs` puts the modes in a top bar,
`navigation.sections` renders them as sidebar groups, `navigation.path` adds breadcrumbs so a
reader arriving from search can see which mode they landed in, and `navigation.prune` helps on
large sites.

`navigation.instant` and instant previews require `site_url`, since they rely on the generated
`sitemap.xml`.

Behaviour for Markdown files present in `docs_dir` but absent from an explicit `nav` is not
documented, and `not_in_nav` is unsupported — verify against your version rather than assuming
MkDocs' build-and-warn behaviour.

---

## Section landing pages

Enable `navigation.indexes` and put the section's `index.md` **first** in its nav array:

```toml
nav = [
  { "How-to guides" = [
    "how-to/index.md",
    { "How to authenticate" = "how-to/authenticate.md" },
    { "How to deploy to Kubernetes" = "how-to/deploy-to-kubernetes.md" },
  ] },
]
```

`README.md` also counts as an index page, but if both `README.md` and `index.md` exist in a
directory the behaviour is currently undefined — pick one.

`navigation.indexes` is **not compatible with `toc.integrate`**.

For the landing page content itself, grids of linked cards work well (Material's card grid
syntax carries over). What matters more than layout is the orienting sentence and the pointer
elsewhere — see `architecture.md`.

---

## Page titles

Precedence, highest first:

1. Title given in `nav`
2. Front matter `title`
3. First `# H1` in the page
4. Base filename

A page with a `nav` title and no `# H1` gets the nav title as its `<h1>`, as in MkDocs.
(Early Zensical releases used the *base filename* instead.) Still give every page an explicit
`# H1`, because the H1 is where the mode signal lives ("How to…") and it travels with the file
when the nav changes.

---

## Front matter

```markdown
---
title: How to authenticate against a private registry
description: Configure credentials for a private package registry.
icon: lucide/key
status: new
tags:
  - authentication
  - registries
---

# How to authenticate against a private registry
```

Recognised keys: `title`, `description`, `icon`, `status` (keyed to `[project.extra.status]`;
built-ins `new` and `deprecated`), `template`, `tags`, `hide` (`navigation`, `toc`, `path`,
`tags`), and `search: {exclude: true}`. Arbitrary keys are available to templates as
`page.meta.*`.

`description` is worth filling in on every page — it becomes the meta description and therefore
the search-result snippet, which is where most readers first judge whether a page is the mode
they need.

---

## Markdown and content features

Python Markdown plus PyMdown Extensions — the same dialect as Material for MkDocs. CommonMark
is explored but not present.

One trap: **Zensical's default extension set differs from MkDocs'** (MkDocs activates only
`meta`, `toc`, `tables`, `fenced_code`). Defaults apply only when you define no
`markdown_extensions` at all — there is no add/remove preset mechanism yet, so the moment you
declare one extension you are declaring all of them. If a migrated project renders oddly, this
is the first thing to check.

Features that carry real weight in a Diátaxis site:

- **Admonitions** for `!!! note` / `!!! tip`, and `pymdownx.details` for collapsible
  `??? note` — good for keeping advanced options out of a how-to's happy path.
- **Content tabs** (`pymdownx.tabbed`) with `content.tabs.link` so a platform choice persists
  site-wide. This is what lets one how-to serve macOS/Linux/Windows instead of three drifting
  copies.
- **Snippets** (`pymdownx.snippets`) to include shared fragments from real files rather than
  transcribing them — the Zensical equivalent of `literalinclude` with sentinels. Use section
  markers, not line ranges.
- **Code annotations** (`content.code.annotate`) — numbered markers inside a code block that
  expand to prose. Excellent in tutorials, where they let you narrate a snippet without breaking
  it up; avoid in reference, where they read as instruction.
- **Definition lists** (`def_list`) for reference entries.
- **Tables**, **footnotes**, **abbreviations** (`abbr`, with a shared glossary file included via
  snippets — a good substitute for Sphinx's `{term}` role).

---

## Link validation

Zensical validates links at build time, on by default, resolving inline and reference-style
links **and anchors**. This is the main safety net for a restructure and it is better than
MkDocs' — use it.

```toml
[project.validation]
invalid_links = "error"
invalid_link_anchors = "error"
```

```bash
zensical build --strict     # exits 1 on validation failure
```

Always link to `.md` files, not built HTML paths — Zensical rewrites them according to
`use_directory_urls`. Linking to `.html` bypasses validation and breaks when that setting changes.

Some `[project.validation]` keys (`unresolved_references`, `unresolved_footnotes`,
`unused_definitions`, `unused_footnotes`, `shadowed_definitions`, `shadowed_footnotes`) are
deprecated in their current form; `invalid_links` and `invalid_link_anchors` are the active ones.
`validation = false` disables everything.

---

## Cross-linking and glossaries

There is no `{term}`/`{ref}` role system. The equivalents:

- **Relative `.md` links** for cross-mode references — validated at build time, so they are safe.
- **Heading anchors** via `toc.permalink = true`; anchors are slugified from heading text, so
  renaming a heading breaks inbound links. Where a link must survive, add an explicit anchor
  (`## Flags {#cli-run-flags}` with `attr_list` enabled).
- **A glossary** via the `abbr` extension plus a snippets-included abbreviations file, so a term
  defined once gets tooltips everywhere. This substitutes for Sphinx's glossary role and solves
  the same duplication problem.

---

## API reference

Zensical supports **mkdocstrings** and **autorefs**, so Python API reference can be generated
into `reference/api/` pages and listed in the nav alongside hand-written reference. `gen-files`
and `literate-nav` are **not** supported, so the common mkdocstrings pattern of generating one
page per module at build time does not work — write the API pages explicitly, one per module or
package, each containing the mkdocstrings directive.

That is more manual than the Sphinx equivalent, but it has an upside worth noting to the user:
explicit pages let you curate what appears in reference and give each a proper title, rather
than dumping the module tree into the nav.

---

## Feature gaps that affect architecture

| Need | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Redirects | Supported: the `redirects` plugin — see the top of this file |
| Tag index/listing pages | Not supported. Tagging pages works (rendered at page bottom, filterable in search) but there are no tag landing pages yet |
| Blog | Not supported |
| Social cards | Not supported |
| `awesome-nav` / `literate-nav` / `.pages` files | Not supported |
| `gen-files` | Not supported |
| `hooks` | Not supported |
| Search UI localisation | English-only at present |
| Versioning | Supported via `mike`, with version warning banner and aliases |
| Offline builds | Supported (`use_directory_urls` forced false) |
| mkdocstrings / autorefs / macros / glightbox | Supported |

If the plan depends on tag-based navigation across modes (e.g. "all pages about
authentication"), note that only search-based filtering is available today.

---

## Migrating from MkDocs

`mkdocs.yml` is read natively and will stay supported as a transition mechanism, so a Diátaxis
restructure and a Zensical migration do not have to happen together — and generally should not.
Do them as separate changes so that when something renders oddly you know which change caused it.

There is **no `zensical migrate` command**; the CLI has only `new`, `build`, `serve`. Converting
`mkdocs.yml` to `zensical.toml` is manual.

Generated HTML is deliberately identical to Material for MkDocs, so existing overrides, CSS and
JS carry over. Two theme variants: `modern` (default) and `classic` (pixel-matches Material).

---

## CLI and CI

```bash
zensical new <dir>
zensical serve --open --dev-addr localhost:8000
zensical build --strict --clean
```

`build` options: `--config-file/-f`, `--clean/-c`, `--strict/-s`. `serve` options:
`--config-file/-f`, `--open/-o`, `--dev-addr/-a`. (`serve --strict` exists but is marked
unsupported.)

CI for a restructure:

```bash
zensical build --strict          # fails on broken internal links and anchors
```

Zensical's own validation covers internal links but not inbound URLs, so also run:

```bash
python <skill-dir>/scripts/check_links.py docs/            # works before the site builds
python <skill-dir>/scripts/make_redirect_stubs.py --map audit/migration-map.md \
    --emit stubs --out site/ --url-style dirhtml            # after zensical build
```

# Talk conventions of this skill's author

These are the house rules of the person who maintains this skill (Nathaniel Starkman), learned from
their talks. Apply them only when the person you are working for says the deck is their own talk or
asks for these conventions. For anyone else, use what is generally useful (checking citations,
notes after a divider, a backup section) and leave the rest.

## Words on slides

- In slide **body text** write "DM", not "dark matter". **Titles** keep the words as the author
  wrote them.
- A constraint or result slide names its source with the paper icon at the **top right**
  (`{{< paper … corner="true" >}}`), not with the paper's name in the title.
- Slides on a field outside the author's expertise get a **light grey background**
  (`{background-color="#efefef"}`) and their notes start with "I'm not an expert here; this is my
  reading of the literature."
- Backup material goes in a **section at the end** (`# Backup` and `{visibility="uncounted"}` slides),
  after the closing slide, never interleaved.

## Speaker notes

- The notes are the author talking: plain first-person spoken sentences, short, pointing at what is
  on screen ("the orange line", "on the left").
- Not: "X isn't Y. It's Z." reveals, slogan one-liners, stacked fragments, a bolded label opening
  every line.
- Extra detail (numbers, caveats, where a figure came from) goes after a `- - -` divider line, below
  what is said aloud.

```markdown
::: {.notes}
Here's every bound on one plane. The grey region on the left is ruled out by microlensing.

- - -

Plane regenerated from the review's public code (scripts/planes.py). Microlensing bound: survey paper, their Fig. 3.
:::
```

## Citations

- Every paper cited in the talk is in the talk's **Zotero collection**; the bibliography slide is
  generated from it (`bibliography.py`), never typed by hand. Add a paper to the collection when you
  cite it.
- Cite on a slide with the `paper` shortcode: "[icon] Name et al. (year)", linking to the DOI.
- **Check before showing**: every citation, arXiv ID, DOI, figure number or label and physical claim is
  checked against its source (open the paper or its arXiv page) before the slide is shown to the
  author. A plausible-looking arXiv ID is not evidence.

## Deck folder

- `git init` the deck folder on day one and commit as you go.
- Keep `.venv/`, cloned data or code repositories and render output out of it (`.gitignore` in the
  template); record how to recreate them in the deck's README instead.
- Delete unused figures as soon as a slide stops using them; regenerate figures from scripts in the
  folder rather than keeping every version. (One talk's folder reached 319 MB this way.)

# Data Model: skills registry

## Skill (the common view of both kinds)

| Field | Local skill | External skill |
|---|---|---|
| name | folder name = `card.json` name = `SKILL.md` name | registry file stem = entry name = `SKILL.md` name at ref |
| description | `card.json` description | entry description |
| origin | `local` | `external` |
| source.repo | `nstarman/skills` | entry `source.repo` |
| source.path | the folder name | entry `source.path` |
| source.ref | `main` | entry `source.ref` (tag or branch) |
| href | `https://github.com/nstarman/skills/tree/main/<name>` | `https://github.com/<repo>/tree/<ref>/<path>` |
| install | `<name>@nstarman-skills` | same |
| zip | `https://github.com/nstarman/skills/releases/latest/download/<name>.zip` | same |

Validation rules (all skills):

- `name` matches `^[a-z0-9-]{1,64}$`; unique across local folders and registry entries.
- card/entry `description`: non-empty string.
- `SKILL.md` frontmatter at the skill's source: `name` equals the skill's name; `description`
  non-empty, at most 1024 characters (claude.ai / Agent Skills limit). `SKILL.md` over 500 lines is
  a warning.

## Registry entry (`registry/<name>.json`)

Exactly the keys `name`, `description`, `source`; `source` exactly `repo` (`owner/repo`), `path`
(relative, no leading `/`, no `..`), `ref` (non-empty). See
[contracts/registry-entry.md](contracts/registry-entry.md).

## Local skill

A top-level folder with `SKILL.md` and `card.json` (exactly `name`, `description`). Folders under
`.claude/`, `.specify/`, `.github/`, `registry/`, `scripts/`, `specs/`, `tests/` are never skills;
only top-level folders containing `SKILL.md` are.

## Index (`index.json`)

`{ "$comment", "schema": 1, "marketplace": "nstarman-skills", "skills": [Skill …] }` sorted by
name. See [contracts/index-json.md](contracts/index-json.md).

## Release

Tag `vYYYY.MM.DD[.N]`; assets: one `<name>.zip` per skill and `hashes.json`
(`{name: sha256-of-zip}`). Published only when `hashes.json` would differ from the latest
release's.

State of a tag-pinned entry: `current` (ref = latest release tag) → `behind` (a newer release tag
exists) → proposed in the weekly pull request → `current` after merge. Branch-tracking entries have
no state.

# Skills registry — agreed design (input to /speckit-plan)

Agreed with the author on 2026-10-21/22, section by section.

## Context

- Today: local skills `<skill>/` (SKILL.md, card.json) in nstarman/skills; `check-cards.yml`
  validates cards; the website's `scripts/collect-skills.mjs` (weekly `refresh-skills.yml`) reads
  `*/card.json` through the GitHub API and writes `config/skills.json` for /tools/.
- Skills elsewhere: `nstarman/quax` `skills/quax`; `GalacticDynamics/unxt` `skills/unxt`
  (nstarman/unxt is a fork without it); `nstarman/figkit` `skills/figkit`, `skills/figkit-upgrade`.
- Approaches considered: registry + generated outputs (chosen); vendored copies (rejected:
  duplication and drift); git submodules (rejected: whole repos, friction, invisible to the API
  collector). Descriptions live in the registry entry for now; deferring to an upstream `card.json`
  may come later.

## 1. Layout and registry format

```
<skill>/                         local skills, unchanged
registry/<name>.json             one per external skill
index.json                       generated
.claude-plugin/marketplace.json  generated
scripts/build_index.py           generator + validator (stdlib Python); release_zips.py, bump_refs.py and the shared skillreg.py beside it (plan)
README.md                        skill table + install section generated between markers
```

```json
{ "name": "unxt", "description": "…",
  "source": { "repo": "GalacticDynamics/unxt", "path": "skills/unxt", "ref": "main" } }
```

Exactly these keys. `name` = file stem = `SKILL.md` name at ref; unique across local + registry.
`ref` is a tag (versioned skills) or a branch (tracking). Initial entries: quax (`nstarman/quax`,
`skills/quax`, `main`); unxt (`GalacticDynamics/unxt`, `skills/unxt`, `main`); figkit and
figkit-upgrade (`nstarman/figkit`, `skills/<name>`, `v0.2.0`). Repo-internal `.github/skills/*`
are not registered.

## 2. Generated outputs and validation

`index.json`:

```json
{ "$comment": "Generated by scripts/build_index.py from */card.json and registry/*.json. Do not edit.",
  "schema": 1, "marketplace": "nstarman-skills",
  "skills": [ { "name": "unxt", "description": "…", "origin": "external",
                "href": "https://github.com/GalacticDynamics/unxt/tree/main/skills/unxt",
                "source": { "repo": "GalacticDynamics/unxt", "path": "skills/unxt", "ref": "main" },
                "install": "unxt@nstarman-skills",
                "zip": "https://github.com/nstarman/skills/releases/latest/download/unxt.zip" } ] }
```

Sorted by name; local `href` = this repo's folder at `main`, local `source` = this repo, `ref` main.

`.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`: name `nstarman-skills`, owner Nathaniel Starkman; one plugin per
skill, plugin name = skill name (skills appear as `/<name>:<name>`); source = the skill folder
itself with `"skills": ["./"]` — `./<name>` for local skills, `git-subdir` (`url` = repo, `path`,
`ref`) for external ones; the entry is the manifest (no plugin.json). Settled by research R1
(validated and installed for local and external skills).

README: table (name, description, from) and install section regenerated between marker comments.

Validation (one workflow replacing `check-cards.yml`, on PR and push): exact keys and non-empty
strings for cards and entries; unique names; local `SKILL.md` name = folder; external `SKILL.md`
fetched at repo/path/ref via the API, name must match; frontmatter limits (name `[a-z0-9-]{1,64}`,
description ≤ 1024 chars; YAML block scalars `>`/`|` parsed); freshness (`build_index.py --check`);
`claude plugin validate .` with the Claude Code CLI installed in CI. Weekly `bump-refs` job:
tag-pinned entries → latest release tag of their repo → one PR updating refs and regenerating.

## 3. Website change (nstarman/nstarman.github.io, separate PR, after this ships)

`scripts/collect-skills.mjs` reads `index.json` (respecting `SKILLS_REF`) instead of scanning
folders; writes `config/skills.json` with `{name, description, href}` plus optional `from`
(external repo); throws and writes nothing on missing/malformed input. /tools/ shows "from
<repo>" for external skills and one "install all" pointer to the README. `refresh-skills.yml`
unchanged (weekly + manual). No cross-repo trigger and no new secrets.

## 4. Zips and releases

Zip = one top-level folder `<name>/` with `SKILL.md` and its resources, without `card.json`;
external skills fetched at their ref. `release.yml`: on pushes to `main` touching skills or the
registry, weekly, and manual; build all zips, compare content hashes with the latest release's,
publish a new release tagged `vYYYY.MM.DD` (suffix `.N` if repeated that day) only when anything
changed. `releases/latest/download/<name>.zip` is the stable link in `index.json`. Only
`GITHUB_TOKEN` with `contents: write`. README install: Claude Code (`/plugin marketplace add
nstarman/skills`, `/plugin install <name>@nstarman-skills`), claude.ai (download zip, upload),
by hand (copy the folder).

Add a registry for skills held in other repositories, and generate from it and the local skill

skill folder itself with `"skills": ["./"]`, verified by installing local and external skills.

## R1. One skill folder as one plugin

- **Decision**: every plugin entry's source is the skill folder itself, with `"skills": ["./"]`:
  a relative path `./<skill>` for local skills, a `git-subdir` source (`url` = repo, `path` = the
  skill folder, `ref`) for external ones. No `plugin.json` anywhere: the entry is the manifest.
- **Evidence**: four entry forms all passed `claude plugin validate` and installed with exactly one
  skill in their component inventory: (A) local folder as root + `skills: ["./"]`; (B) repo root +
  `skills: ["./diataxis"]`; (C) external `git-subdir` to the `skills/` parent + `skills: ["./quax"]`;
  (D) external `git-subdir` to the skill folder at tag `v0.2.0` + `skills: ["./"]`.
- **Why A/D**: they copy only the skill's folder into the plugin cache; B copies the whole repo, C
  the who

tag of its repository
  (`git ls-remote --tags`); for those, the latest release's `tag_name` (`/repos/<repo>/releases/latest`)

# Data model: syw-adopt-overleaf

## Backup folder

`~/backups/<old-repo>-<YYYY-MM-DD>/` (outside Dropbox and iCloud; `backup.sh`
refuses a path under either):

| File | Content | Verified by |
|---|---|---|
| `repo.bundle` | `git bundle create --all` of the old repository | `git bundle verify` |
| `mirror.tar.gz` | the Dropbox mirror folder | `tar -tzf` lists every file (count matches) |
| `overleaf/` | clone of the Overleaf git remote, no secret in its config (research R3) | `git fsck`, no `olp_`/token in `.git/config` |
| `baseline.pdf` | the paper compiled before the migration (R7) | `pdfinfo` reads it |
| `secrets.txt` | `gh secret list` of the old repository: names and dates only | exists (may list none) |
| `MIGRATION.md` | the migration record (below) | — |

The folder must not exist beforehand (no overwriting a previous backup).

## Inventory

A tab-separated file `inventory.tsv` in the backup folder, one line per Overleaf file, `#`
comments allowed:

```text
<class>\t<path relative to the Overleaf r
…[内容超出评审预算——仅保留首尾各 1024 字符]…
ctions, filled as the migration goes (template in `references/migration-template.md`):

1. **Sources** — old repository, mirror path, Overleaf project id, slug, new repository.
2. **Findings** — survey notes (submodules, custom `\variable`, build system, data locations).
3. **Inventory** — counts per class; points to `inventory.tsv`.
4. **Gates** — one line per ⛔: phase, what was shown, the author's answer, date.
5. **Freeze** — Overleaf commit at the freeze; at the first sync (must match, or reconcile).
6. **PDF differences** — each `pdf_diff.py` run: what differed, the author's decision.
7. **Push / pull lists** — the drafted `overleaf:` block and the `check_lists.py` result.
8. **Prune list** — the approved class-4 deletions.

## Phase state

Phases 0–8 run in order; a phase starts only when the previous phase's gate (if any) has a
recorded yes in `MIGRATION.md`. The old repository's state changes only in phase 8 (archived).
The Overleaf project changes only in phases 6 (rename, first push) and 7 (prune).

# Research: quarto-revealjs

Decisions behind the skill, each with the evidence that settled it. All observations: Quarto

## R1. Authoring pipeline: Quarto → reveal.js, PDF from the same HTML

- **Decision**: author in Quarto (`format: revealjs`, `embed-resources: true`); print the PDF with
  reveal.js's own print view (`?print-pdf`).

Evidence is the talk folder (kept private; its scripts are the working reference) and the

## R1. Inlining background-iframe apps

- **Decision**: after rendering, embed each referenced local app as base64 in a
  `<script type="text/plain">`, and a small script, placed before `Reveal.initialize`, builds a
  `blob:` URL and rewrites `data-background-iframe` and iframe `src`/`data-src` to it.
- **Rationale**: Quarto's `embed-resources` leaves `data-background-iframe` as a path. A `data:` URL
  in its place loaded but stayed blank for a real app (opaque origin); `blob:` URLs keep the
  page's origin. Running before reveal.js initialises means no request for the path is ever made.
- **Alternatives**: `data:` URL (blank for apps needing an origin); shipping `apps/` beside the deck
  (not one file); inline `<iframe>` (fine for simple apps, but also a `data:` URL).

## R2. `<object data=…>`

- **Decision**: the same step swaps a local `<object

e offline and
  overflow checks accept `--webkit`; the PDF stays Chromium (`page.pdf` is Chromium-only).

## R6. Browser launch

- **Decision**: `headless=True` explicitly; try `channel="chrome"`, fall back to Playwright's bundled
  Chromium when Chrome is missing.
- **Rationale**: the author's rule: never a visible browser window; CI and fresh machines may lack

## R7. Citations

- **Decision**: a shortcode extension `paper` (`url`, `who`, `year`, `title`, `corner`) emitting one
  link "[icon] who (year)", or the icon alone placed top-right; icon as a `data:` CSS mask in the
  extension's CSS, inlined by `embed-resources`. `bibliography.py` writes the same shortcodes from a

- **Alternatives**: raw `[[]{.icon}](url){.paper-ref}` Markdown as in the talk (verbose, easy to
  get wrong); Quarto citations with CSL (no icon, no corner form, needs a `.bib` export).

# Mapping an Overleaf project onto the SYW layout

SYW's `src/tex/` mirrors the Overleaf project root: `src/tex/figures/<group>/a.pdf` is
`figures/<group>/a.pdf` in Overleaf. Every Overleaf file goes in exactly one class.

| Class | What | Repository | `showyourwork.yml` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Text | authored in Overleaf: `ms.tex`, `bib.bib` (after the rename), any `\input` sections | `src/tex/`, committed | `pull` |
| 2. Build output | made by code: `figures/**/*.pdf`, `output/**.tex` | `src/tex/figures`, `src/tex/output`, gitignored, regenerated | `push` |
| 3. Static support | needed to compile, not generated: `.cls`, `.bst`, logos, `preamble/*.sty` | `src/tex/`, committed | `push` (the repository is the source of truth) |
| 4. Not needed in Overleaf | code, data, lockfiles, notes, referee replies | code → `src/scripts`, data → `src/data`; private notes stay out of git | neither; pruned in phase 7 |

# Building a showyourwork paper locally

## Environment

- Run `showyourwork build` from a shell where the conda environment that contains
  `snakemake` and `showyourwork` is on `PATH`, for example
  `export PATH="$HOME/miniconda3/envs/showyourwork-main/bin:$PATH"`.
- Analysis code usually runs through `uv run --locked python ...` inside Snakemake rules.
  If the repo has no `.venv` yet (a fresh clone or a moved folder), the first rule creates it
  and needs network access.
- Pin the Python version the lockfile supports with a `.python-version` file (for example
  `3.12`). A new machine's `uv` may pick the newest CPython, for which scientific wheels
  (jaxlib, ...) do not exist yet, and the environment fails to install.

## The command

```sh
export PYTHONPATH=src            # see gotchas: macOS hides .pth files
showyourwork build \
  --cores 2 \
  --rerun-incomplete \
  --conda-not-block-search-path-envvars
```

Add `--scheduler greedy` on Apple Silicon without Rosetta: Snakemake's default
(MILP) scheduler r
…[内容超出评审预算——仅保留首尾各 1024 字符]…
it in the background, redirect output to a log file, and watch the log for the final
`Pushing changes to Overleaf` / `Done!` or for `Error` / `Traceback`. Expect minutes for a
warm cache and much longer when a cached rule must be recomputed. Do not start a second
build or a second Overleaf push while one is running: both use the same git clone under
`.showyourwork/overleaf` and can collide.

## What invalidates caches

Cached rules are keyed on their inputs, including any settings file (for example
`variables.yml`) that is listed as an input. Editing that file, even a comment, can force
an expensive recompute and a round trip to Zenodo. For hours-long computations, keep a
committed backup of the result and a `local_cache:` switch in `showyourwork.yml` that copies
the backup instead of recomputing, with a fingerprint test that fails when the backup no
longer matches its sources. Re-record fingerprints only when a change cannot affect the
physics (for example, adding an unrelated section to the settings file).

# Gotchas, with causes

Each entry is a symptom, why it happens, and what to do.

## Builds that stall or hang

- **Idle for many minutes right after `Syncing file with Zenodo ... cache`, no CPU, no child
  process.** `SANDBOX_TOKEN` (or the Zenodo token) is not set; the sync fails and then waits
  forever. Interrupt (`kill -INT <pid>`) and rerun with the token. Say so in the project README.
- **Looks hung at `Updating checkpoint dependencies` for an hour or more.** Not a deadlock:
  SYW walks each output's upstream dependencies recursively and runs `git` per edge. With
  dozens of `\variable{}` outputs it takes hours. Memoize
  `showyourwork.config.expand_dependency_directories` (for example with
  `functools.lru_cache`) at the top of the `Snakefile`.
- **A build that never starts.** The password-manager CLI is blocked on a locked app:
  `op read` waits silently. Unlock the app and retry. Check that `op` is using the intended
  account (`--account <domain>` or `OP_ACCOUNT`).
- **`Overleaf credential OVERLEAF
…[内容超出评审预算——仅保留首尾各 1024 字符]…
 in `showyourwork cache restore`, on a figure.** A cached rule's output is
  a symlink into `.showyourwork/cache`. Under `src/tex/figures` the GitHub Actions article cache
  saves the link without its target, and the next run crashes on it. Write cached outputs under
  `src/data/` and copy them into `src/tex/figures/` with a plain `cp` rule; bump the action's
  `article-cache-number` to drop the saved cache.
- **A figure CI pushed to Overleaf has a different size from the local one.** A script that
  measures text in pixels (`fig.canvas.draw()`, `get_window_extent()`) before
  `bbox_inches="tight"` depends on the DPI, and matplotlib's default backend differs: `macosx`
  on a Retina Mac draws at 200 dpi, Agg on CI at 100. Pin it in the script:
  `matplotlib.use("agg")` and `plt.figure(..., dpi=200)`. Check with `pdfinfo` (page size).
- **Pytest hangs or starts a long computation.** `--doctest-modules` over `src/` imports every
  figure script, which runs it. Point `testpaths` at the package and `tests/` only.

# Quoting numbers: the `\variable{}` plumbing

The text never contains a typed result. A result goes through four steps:

1. A `calc_*.py` script computes it and writes it with `write_values(__file__, {...})` into a
   JSON file under `src/data/derived/`.
2. An exporter script (`make_variables.py`) reads those JSON files and `variables.yml` and
   renders each number as a one-line `.tex` file (`src/tex/output/<group>/<name>.tex`),
   choosing the format (significant figures, percent, a range) in one place.
3. `ms.tex` cites it as `\variable{output/<group>/<name>.tex}`.
4. SYW generates only the variables `ms.tex` cites, and pushes them to Overleaf at the end of
   a build.

Consequences:

- A new number needs: the value in a `calc_*` script, a line in the exporter, the citation in
  the text, and a build. Until the build has pushed, Overleaf cannot compile the citation.
- To change how a number looks, change the exporter, not the text.
- Constants that define a model or a test (a halo shape, a radius range) belong in
  `variables.yml` and are cited from there, so the paper and the code cannot disagree.
- Describe what a number is in the text, and let the variable carry its value. If you must
  quote a computed number in chat, quote it from the generated file, not from memory.

# Contract: the skill's scripts

All in `syw-adopt-overleaf/scripts/`; standard-library Python 3.11+ or POSIX sh/Bash, plus `git`,
`gh`, `op`, poppler where noted. Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 check failed / differences found, 2 usage or
tool error. Nothing prints a token.

## `backup.sh`

```text
backup.sh --repo <old repo clone> --mirror <Dropbox mirror folder> --overleaf-id <id>
          --op-ref <op://… Overleaf token> --baseline <baseline.pdf> [--dest <backups root>]
```

- `--dest` defaults to `~/backups`; the folder `<old-repo>-<YYYY-MM-DD>` is
  created and must not exist. Refuses a destination under Dropbox or iCloud
  (`~/Library/CloudStorage`, `~/Library/Mobile Documents`).
- Writes and verifies the five parts (data-model.md), printing one `ok <part>` line each; on the
  first failure prints `FAILED <part>: <reason>` and exits 1, leaving what was written for
  inspection.
- Reads the repository, the mirror and Overleaf only; writes only inside the new folder.

## `pdf_diff.py`

```text
pdf_diff.py <baselin
…[内容超出评审预算——仅保留首尾各 1024 字符]…
N>: <old> → <new>`.
- With `--out`, writes `p<N>-baseline.png` and `p<N>-new.png` for each flagged page.
- Exit 0 only when every section is `same`.

## `check_lists.py`

```text
check_lists.py <overleaf block or showyourwork.yml> <inventory.tsv>
```

- Applies research R4's three rules; prints `ok` or one `FAIL <rule>: <path>` line per problem.

## `public_check.sh`

```text
public_check.sh <new repo> <repo.bundle> <inventory.tsv>
```

- Research R6: shared commits, token-like strings in history, private class-4 paths in history. Prints
  `ok <check>` or `FAIL <check>: <detail>` (a token match prints commit and path, never the match).
- Read-only on the new repository.

## `syw-overleaf-dropbox/scripts/check_build.sh` (changed)

- Same usage and output lines; figures are found with `find src/tex/figures -name '*.pdf'`, and
  each is compared with the mirror file at the same relative path
  (`src/tex/figures/sub/a.pdf` ↔ `<mirror>/figures/sub/a.pdf`). Output names the relative path
  (`figure sub/a.pdf: …`).

# About the architecture

Why is a run single-threaded? Because the design favours reproducible output over speed: the
reason is that parallel writers would make the order of rows depend on timing. The trade-off is
that large runs are slower, which is why `--jobs` exists (see the [CLI flags](../reference/cli.md#flags)).

# CLI

## Flags

| Flag | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--dry-run` | bool | `false` | Parse and validate only. |
| `--jobs` | int | `1` | Number of worker processes. |

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Success. |
| 1 | The pipeline failed. |

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `source.url` | string | none | Where the dataset is fetched from. |
| `output.partition_by` | list of strings | `[]` | Columns to partition the output by. |

# Build your first pipeline

In this tutorial we will build a pipeline that fetches a dataset and publishes it.
By the end of this tutorial you will have a published dataset.

1. First, create `pipeline.toml`.
2. Next, run `toolkit run pipeline.toml`.
3. Finally, open `out/index.html`. You should see one table.

Congratulations. You used `toolkit run`; its flags are in the
[CLI reference](../reference/cli.md#flags). Curious why runs are single-threaded? Read
